neighbours.summary: The crusader who holds Lavaur in 1220. He admits Na Geralda's killing was a crime and wants her bones and her memory left undisturbed; he and his men will turn on anyone who tries to lay her ghost, which they cannot see and do not believe in.

neighbours.name: Lambert de Thury
neighbours.summary: The crusader who has ruled Castle Puivert since it fell to de Montfort in 1210, taking it from Bernard of Congost. His wife, the Lady de Thury, keeps the castle's custom of welcoming troubadours, and with it the jealousy of the lake's faerie lady.

neighbours.name: Bouchard de Marly
neighbours.summary: De Montfort's kinsman and loyal friend, who spent sixteen months chained in the dungeons of Cabaret until its surrender in 1211, and whose relief column was routed at St. Martin-Lalande. He holds Saissac in 1220 against its dispossessed heirs.

neighbours.name: Pierre-Roger de Cabaret
neighbours.summary: The faidit lord of the three castles of Lastours, a friend of the Cathars and a lavish host to troubadours, who had to surrender them in 1211 but was never caught. He is working to get his lands and fortresses back, and with the crusade faltering he may succeed. His brother Jourdain, lord of Pennautier, is husband of Na Loba.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Toulouse
neighbours.summary:
Foulques de Marseille, among the most powerful and divisive men in the region, hated by most of Toulouse, even former friends of the Church. A celebrated troubadour in his youth, he turned from his old life after a vision twenty-five years ago, and now weeps and does harsh penance whenever a song of his reaches his ears, appalled that his sins outlive him. As a churchman he fights the south's easy morals and has three great hates, heretics, troubadours and moneylenders, and since many lenders are Jews he has come to dislike the Jews.

He backs Dominic's preaching mission. Replacing a corrupt, indifferent predecessor, he needed the pope's help to take his cathedral and an armed guard at all times, and grew to return the city's hatred; by the time the crusade was called he could no longer safely enter his see, and joined the crusaders. Count Raimond tried to win him, even giving him the Château Narbonnais, but they became bitter enemies. In 1220 he rides with the crusaders, pressing for Toulouse to be captured and the heretics wiped out, and he favours an Inquisition of clerical investigators to hunt heresy. In 1209 he founded the White Brotherhood.

He knows of the Order and, through dealings with the Quaesitor Augustus, respects it, but has no idea of its real power or of its Cathar magi; he thinks the scholars of Toulouse practise natural magic. Proof of heretic magi against his faith would make him a terrible enemy of the Order and add it to the crusade's targets unless the pope forbade it.
neighbours.secrets: As a young man he went to Tolosa Paratge as a gifted troubadour; his mind may have been magically changed afterwards, or he may have put it down to a dream. He is a great latent danger to the Order in the south.

neighbours.name: Arnaud Amalric, Papal Legate
neighbours.summary:
For twenty years the leading figure in the Church's effort to reclaim the south from heresy, a Cistercian of great learning who rode with de Montfort, presided over the burning of Cathars and the massacre of those who resisted, and is credited with the notorious order at Béziers to kill everyone and let God sort out his own. Made bishop (archbishop) of Narbonne in 1212, he has defended the local Church against northern appointees, and he never supported French claims to the land.

In 1220 he has made peace with Count Raimond, convinced at last of his piety and alarmed at the threat the French crown poses to southern culture; he keeps a soft spot for Alice and Amaury de Montfort while standing hard against the French push south. Since de Montfort's death he has befriended the young knight Carolus St. Tropez and often stays at his castle of Pujol. He thinks the Order a loose fellowship of scholars and natural magicians, and likes it as long as it heeds the Church; if he found it sheltering heretics he would turn the curia against it unless it cast them out.
neighbours.secrets: He does not know St. Tropez is a magus, and St. Tropez's influence has hardened him against the French and woken his southern sympathies.

neighbours.name: Basilica of Saint-Sernin
neighbours.summary: The great pilgrim church of Toulouse, kept by Augustinian canons under their compassionate abbot Jordan Giordano, who runs its college and the hospice for the city's poor. Summer brings crowds of pilgrims to its relics, and a poetry contest is held in its orchard.

neighbours.name: Saint-Pierre des Cuisines
neighbours.summary: The oldest church site in the Tribunal, rebuilt two centuries ago and owned by the monks of Moissac: the poor relation of the city's churches, yet the place where the counts hold court and swear to the people and the capitouls proclaim their laws. Its steps hold a Magic lacuna of aura 1.

neighbours.name: Our Lady of the Sea Bream (La Daurade)
neighbours.summary: A domed basilica of twelve walls glittering with gold mosaic, built on a Roman temple of Apollo and attached to a Benedictine monastery, home of the Black Madonna, Notre-Dame Noire. It hosts the flower procession and feast each early May. In history the Saint-Sernin poetry contest moves here within the decade and grows into the Festival of the Flowers, with gold and silver flowers for the best Occitan verse.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Carcassonne (St Nazaire)
neighbours.summary: A Romanesque cathedral, which some crusaders want rebuilt in the Gothic style, holding the tomb of Simon de Montfort. The northern lords prefer clergy who came with the crusade, and many local priests have lost their posts and gone over to the Trencavel heir. Gui de Vaux-de-Cernay was made bishop in 1212, replacing Bernard Raimond de Roquefort, dismissed for sympathy with the Cathars (his mother and brother among them), but Bernard still claims the see and disputes Gui's appointment. Gui defrocked the treacherous priest of Montreal at Bram.
neighbours.secrets: On the feast of Saint Nazarius Gui may suddenly cry out from the altar that he is a usurper and hand his mitre to Bishop Raimond, then at sunset claim he was bewitched and accuse Raimond of sorcery.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Saint Cecilia, Albi
neighbours.summary: The stone cathedral that towers over red-brick Albi, though few of the townsfolk come to Mass.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Benoît, Castres
neighbours.summary: The Benedictine monastery round which Castres grew. In 1209 two Cathar Good Men handed over by the consuls were burned in the market, the crusade's first Cathar victims; one had recanted, and the clergy burned him anyway lest his repentance be false, but his chains fell away in the flames and he walked out unhurt, and was spared.

neighbours.name: Nunnery of St. Marie, Prouille
neighbours.summary: The house Dominic founded below Fanjeaux as a home for converted Cathar women and for girls with a calling, while he preached from Fanjeaux between 1206 and 1215.

neighbours.name: Monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, Villeneuve
neighbours.summary: Built by Odo de Morlhon after a vision on crusade bade him found a house in honour of the Holy Sepulchre; it is now under Cluny.

neighbours.name: Templar Commandery of Villedieu-du-Temple
neighbours.summary: The Templars here buried Baudouin of Toulouse after one of their knights cut him down from the gallows. They keep largely out of the war, though their sympathies are with the crusaders.

neighbours.name: Toulouse
neighbours.summary: One of the largest and richest cities in Mythic Europe, ruled in practice by its twelve capitouls, two from each of six districts, elected every seven years (or on a death) by householders of good standing who meet a wealth test. Raimond IV set up a chapter of four lawyers, two judges and six sheriffs in 1154 to judge trade and law for him, in return for unnamed favours from the Order, whose Tribunals it copies; in 1188 the elected sheriffs threw out the lawyers and judges and took over the guard, the militia, war, taxes and trade, and Raimond V let it pass. They sit in the Capitole, houses bought in 1190 and knocked into one, hearing petitions, trade disputes, taxes, guild law and justice; a simple majority makes a law, and a favourable ruling often takes wealth, influence or a story to earn. Former capitouls are treated as minor nobility for life and keep the title 'sheriff'. Held in 1220 by Count Raimond VI.
neighbours.ruler: The Capitole, under Count Raimond VI

neighbours.name: Albi
neighbours.summary: A red-brick town on the Tarn and an old Cathar stronghold, which met the legate Alberic of Ostia with drums, donkeys and jeers. St Bernard won many over for a while, but the heresy is still strong despite the garrison Simon de Montfort put there. Held in 1220 by a crusader garrison.

neighbours.name: Castres
neighbours.summary: A fortified town round the abbey of St. Benoît between the Agout and the Durenque, its upper storeys jutting out over the water. Its consuls surrendered to de Montfort in September 1209, handing over two Cathars, and still favour the crusade, looking to France and the Montforts rather than to the Trencavel heir. Held in 1220 by its consuls, for the Montforts.
neighbours.ruler: Its consuls, loyal to the Montforts

neighbours.name: Lavaur
neighbours.summary: A small Trencavel town on the Agout with a cathedral of St Alan, infamous as a nest of heresy, stormed in 1211 with terrible slaughter; now a crusader stronghold. Held in 1220 by Gui de Lucy for the crusade.

neighbours.name: Agen
neighbours.summary:
The chief town of the county's wooded, sheep-rearing north, prosperous on fine wool, where the heretics are very strong. The book does not say who holds it in 1220.

An unremarkable town on the Way, home to a small Christian sect, the Valerenes, who say they descend from a Diedne magus who slipped away from the Order by giving up his magic and turning hermit some years before the Schism War. Devoted to St Valerie of Limoges, whom he was said to have known in life, he is remembered by his followers, who each midsummer light candles at Saint Caprasius and then walk to her bones at Limoges and at the Benedictine house of Chambon-sur-Voueize. They live apart in the Gascon wilds, at their founder's old covenant (Bachlach's Hermitage), looking for plain signs of the Divine in nature, and are eager for news of the unicorns of Bazas. They have shown powers of Intervention and Purity, Saint's Aid and Wilderness Sense; their rites are secret, and some say they act out Valerie's beheading. They help the larger Valerene cult of Limoges with great initiations, and both want the ring of Valerie, called so at Richard I's investiture as prince of Aquitaine in 1172 and given back to the bishop of Limoges when Richard took the cross: her refused wedding ring.

neighbours.name: Cahors
neighbours.summary: A city notorious for its moneylenders, in the Jewish quarter and outside it, condemned by the Church. Since Toulouse banned mortgages and loans at the Church's insistence about twenty years ago, Cahors is where one goes to raise money fast. Its towns live by the black wine. The book does not say who holds it in 1220.

neighbours.name: Montcuq
neighbours.summary: A Cathar stronghold with a small castle, taken by de Montfort in summer 1212 and handed to Raimond's brother Baudouin, who had taken the crusaders' side against his own family. It went back to the Toulousain cause, and Baudouin was brought here captive from Lolmie in 1214. Held in 1220 for Count Raimond.

neighbours.name: Montauban
neighbours.summary: The town outside whose walls Baudouin of Toulouse was hanged from a walnut tree for treason in 1214, as Raimond and the Count of Foix looked on. Held in 1220 for Count Raimond.

neighbours.name: Carcassonne
neighbours.summary: A great city of the Trencavels, often defiant of its lords (it drove them out in 1107 and from 1120 to 1124) and called ungovernable, yet loyal to Viscount Raimond-Roger until he was taken by treachery in 1209. It is named, they say, for Lady Carcas, a Saracen commander's wife who under Charlemagne's siege fed the last grain to the last pig and flung it over the wall, so that the besiegers, seeing grain burst from it, gave up on a city so well fed. In 1220 it has one Visigothic wall over Roman work and an eleventh-century stone castle. Almost all its people were driven out after the fall, but most came back, and as the crusaders' base it prospers; resentment of the northerners runs high, but with so many knights quartered there rising would be hopeless. Held in 1220 by Amaury de Montfort.

neighbours.name: Bram
neighbours.summary: A small walled town whose hundred defenders were blinded and mutilated after a three-day siege; its market keeps an Infernal aura of 3. The book does not say who holds it in 1220, but it fell to the crusade.

neighbours.name: Fanjeaux
neighbours.summary: A town on a hill crowned by a small castle, once a heretic stronghold and Dominic's home while he preached; its people fled the crusaders in 1209, and now nobody there dares shelter a Cathar. The book does not name its lord in 1220; the town sides with the Church and the crusade.

neighbours.name: The White Brotherhood
neighbours.summary: A society of Toulousain citizens Bishop Foulques raised in 1209 to take up arms against heretics and moneylenders, oppose Count Raimond and back the crusade, named for the white robes and hoods they wore for their midnight arrests and terror. Loyal to the Church but also to their city, they broke when the bishop and many clergy slipped away during de Montfort's siege, and many, fearing another Béziers, fought the crusaders. Guilty of murder, lynching and riot, they are now a small, violent fanatical core that still prowls the streets at night; their legacy is a strong hatred of Jews among former Whites and the ban on usury. Membership can be the Flaw Dark Secret.

details.wants: Heresy and usury rooted out of Toulouse

neighbours.name: The Black Brotherhood
neighbours.summary: Formed in answer to the White Brotherhood, mostly from the suburbs and the countryside, it fought the Whites in the streets to protect Cathars and Jews, and committed atrocities of its own. Since the siege ended it has dwindled to a small, violent fanatical core that still lurks in the streets after dark. Membership can be the Flaw Dark Secret.

details.wants: The Cathars and Jews of Toulouse protected from the Whites

neighbours.name: The Whites of Tolosa Paratge
neighbours.summary: The faction of Tolosa Paratge that sides with Bishop Foulques and would expel the heretics for bringing ruin on their sodales: St. Tropez, Adam Carpentiere and the grogs and covenfolk who rallied to St. Tropez's white banner. Too afraid to enter the regio, they keep laboratories and a fortified tower in the city and try to blockade the island, waiting to retake it by appeal to the Tribunal in 1221 or by Wizard's War. The White Brotherhood counted some magi among its supporters.

details.wants: The Gorgiastic Cathars expelled from the covenant, then from the city

neighbours.name: The Blacks of Tolosa Paratge
neighbours.summary: The stronger faction of Tolosa Paratge, holding the regio and favouring the Cathar cause: Cyprian, who leads it though no Cathar, and the Gorgiastic Cathar Raimond, with about six grogs and a dozen covenfolk besieged on the island, fearing to leave and waiting for the next Wizard's War. The Black Brotherhood counted some magi among its supporters.

details.wants: The Gorgiastic Cathars kept safe from the Whites and the crusade

neighbours.name: The Faidits
neighbours.summary: Knights and minor lords stripped of their lands by the crusade, landless and lordless, sheltering in castles such as Aguilar, Puilaurens and Cabaret and in friendly villages; in 1220 they are coming home, as the sons of Termes are. Among them are Pons de Morlhon, counselled by the ghosts of seven Waldensian martyrs, Pierre-Roger de Cabaret, and the heirs of Saissac. The Hermetic exiles of Aguilar call themselves Hermetic faidits, and many faidits serve them as companions.

details.wants: Their lands back, by papal favour or by the sword

neighbours.name: Na Loba and her Daughters
neighbours.summary: Auda, called Na Loba, the She-Wolf, once the beauty of Fleur Epine, and her three daughters, who have a strong claim to the castles of Lastours. With no Trencavel overlord left to answer to, the daughters seek husbands rather than wait for them, and use their dark allure to snare good husbands, while the old woman remains a formidable schemer; they travel the country looking for powerful allies.

details.wants: Their birthright, the three castles of Lastours

neighbours.secrets: Peasants whisper that the daughters are werewolves, and anyone who says so soon vanishes. Na Loba betrayed Raimond-Roger Trencavel to de Montfort in 1209 out of jealousy.

neighbours.name: The Moneylenders of Cahors
neighbours.summary: The moneylenders of Cahors, Jewish and Christian, who took over the business of lending when Toulouse outlawed it; Bishop Foulques loathes them, and the former Whites threaten the Jews among them. Adam Carpentiere of Tolosa Paratge owes them a large sum.

details.wants: Their loans honoured and their trade left alone

neighbours.name: Gascony
neighbours.summary:
The Tribunal's western third in 1220: Guyenne and Gascony, reckoned part of the duchy of Aquitaine, a wedge of wild country that runs from Bordeaux up the Garonne and south-east to Charlemagne's Cross by Roncevaux, and takes in the whole Atlantic shore down to Bayonne. Three settled districts cluster round its three cities: Bordeaux in the north; Auch, the archbishop's seat on high ground toward Toulouse; and Bayonne in the south-west, where Gascon country gives way to Basque. Between them lie untilled moor, forest and marsh.

The English crown has held the province hard ever since Richard the Lionheart settled at Bayonne and broke the local barons. The dukes have always ruled from Bordeaux and left the rest alone save for the odd show of strength down the Garonne; young Henry III comes to visit his mother Isabella, who lives close by.

The Way of St James, after Rome and Jerusalem the most travelled pilgrimage in Mythic Europe, crosses much of the duchy on good roads. Of its five routes through the Tribunal, four (the coastal English Way through Bordeaux and Bayonne, the Via Turonensis from Paris by Tours, the Via Lemovicensis from Vézelay by Limoges, and the Via Podiensis from Le Puy, called the Via Gebennensis by those starting at Geneva) meet at Ostabat before the climb to Roncevaux; only the Via Tolosana from Arles, which Italians favour, takes another pass. Palmers wear the scallop shell, keep journals of their stops, and find hospitals, hostels and churches with relics all along the way; Aymeric Picaud's Liber Peregrinationis made the journey famous. Military orders hold commanderies on donated land to guard them and to raise money for the Holy Land: the Templars have twenty in Gascony.

When Innocent III laid England under interdict in 1208, Gascony fell under it as the king's land, and many of its churches stood shut for six years. In the empty interior, far from the pilgrim roads, a band of six demons took root, and Infernal auras are common still: even in towns the Dominion holds by day, the Infernal often takes the night. The interdict left Divine auras weak or strange, and none below 7 is more than six years old.

The six spirits arrived with the interdict, each bent on one deadly sin. A demon settles on a community, possesses its leading people and through them draws the rest into sin until an Infernal aura closes over the place; a host who dies unrepentant comes back as a lesser demon or a ghost. Greed has gone to the bridge of St Thibery, and Gluttony and Wrath ride with the armies in the Narbonnais and the Toulousain, but three remain in Gascony. Cenodoxus Superbia, Lord of Pride and Envy (Infernal Might 40, a lord of the Vessels of Iniquity), plays the patron and muse to craftsmen, swelling their pride and then spreading a contagious envy among those around them until whole guilds rot; he appears as a well-dressed man or woman with a dagger and fine tools, leaves the dagger lying about when tempers run high, can lend a craftsman a great Characteristic or a bonus to his craft for a price, and is strong enough to pass many an Aegis; eight pawns of Vim lie in his tongue and eyes. Julian (or Julia), the Tempter of the Way (Infernal Might 15), a raven-haired young rogue in pilgrim's dress, draws the devout aside, seduces them, travels with them and contrives that they are caught in the act at the worst moment; he rides his victims by night, and three pawns of Vim lie in his belt buckle. Both keep to crowded places: Bordeaux, Bayonne and the ferry at Blaye. Adrian, the Voice of Safety (Infernal Might 30, a spirit of deceit), wanders from inn to inn as a handsome troubadour or trobairitz with a guitar, singing of the horrors done in the name of faith and breeding the sloth of acedia: no one should go on crusade, nor defend the Cathars either, for it would ruin their families and only fatten the nobles; six pawns of Vim lie in his hands, and crusaders are proof against him.

The faeries of the region, from the courtly fae to nymphs, sirens, trolls and fauns, are called the Dames Blanches, and all own Oriande la Fée of Rosefleur in the Médoc as their queen, though most pay her only lip service until she comes in person. Drakes and worms have lately begun to harry pilgrims, worst near Ostabat.

The Basques have lived in the south-west since before Rome; they are expert whalers and hardy fighters, and their customs are the heart of the land. About fifteen folk witches, the sorginak, are scattered through the villages of Gascony and the Basque country, and most defer to Dama of Merinita at Mimizan. They keep the old faith in Mari and in her consort Sugaar, the serpent, whose name Dama's familiar wears among them.

neighbours.name: The True Mithraeum of Bordeaux
neighbours.summary: A natural cavern under the southern quarter of Bordeaux.
neighbours.secrets:
Roman soldiers of the garrison made it a temple of Mithras, and it has lain buried and forgotten for centuries. Only Kaeso of Flambeau knew where it was: fearing the barbarians then holding Bordeaux would find it, he told no one in the Order and built a second temple upriver, where Castra Solis now stands, so that the true one kept its power undimmed. Most Flambeau believe the temple under Castra Solis is Kaeso's own. The book gives no aura for the true one.

Many high initiates of the Legion of Mithras believe their rumoured Great Temple lies somewhere in France.

neighbours.name: Belin
neighbours.summary:
A small hamlet on the Leyre south of Bordeaux, with a keep and a church; folk say Eleanor of Aquitaine was born here. A generous charter draws craftsmen, and Henry III likes to stay in the castle when he visits.

Olivier de Viennes, Ogier the Dane and others of Charlemagne's Twelve Peers lie in the church. The churchyard has a Divine aura of 4 and smells strongly of something very sweet: on the anniversary of Ogier's death the scent can heal a sick penitent, and on the anniversary of Roncevaux it carries 5 pawns of Divine-tempered Creo vis, held by no covenant. Ogier's sword Cortana, of the same steel as Durendal and once Tristan's, is gone from his tomb: Oriande la Fée claims to have it.

neighbours.name: The Médoc
neighbours.summary:
The triangle of country west and north of Bordeaux between the Atlantic and the mouth of the Gironde, mostly marsh and wet ground. Rome kept a post here to guard the coast road; in the ninth century a castle of white limestone, Blanquefort, rose on its ruins to watch two roads: the Levade from Bordeaux north to Soulac, and the Channel Soulac south to Bayonne, the main artery of the English Way of St James, which runs from Soulac to St Jean Pied-de-Port to join the other routes before Roncevaux.

Hundreds of dolmens are strewn through its fens, their Faerie auras ranging from 1 up to 5. Most house faeries of the Dames Blanches who serve the Queen of Rosefleur in tormenting pilgrims, and the stronger beings lair at the stronger stones. Trolls among them try to lure travellers off the road to eat them; others coax pilgrims to live wild until the weather kills them; others only ask for a dance or a small service before letting a traveller by, and plague those who refuse. They wear the shapes known all over Mythic Europe, so every pilgrim recognises their tales.

The inner circle of Dama's cult meets in the Médoc, in the realm of its faerie queen.

neighbours.name: Rosefleur
neighbours.summary:
A faerie castle in a regio of six levels on the western shore near the tip of the Médoc: slender towers, streaming banners and smooth dressed stone amid a paradise of beasts and flowers, nothing like the wet, wind-scoured land at the mundane level. The aura climbs from 2 at the edge to 7 at the castle's heart. Its people go naked most of the time and put on gossamer court dress when their queen receives guests. On the mundane level one can still trace the footings of the little shrine where the Gauls worshipped her as a form of Sirona, goddess of healing and springs.

Oriande la Fée (Faerie Might 50, Herbam; 60 within her own demesne) claims lordship from the north bank of the Gironde south to the Pyrenees and east to the Camargue. Once a giver of gifts, she remade herself as a challenger on the Roman roads and then the Way of St James, drawing vitality from the stories she forces on knights and pilgrims: she makes them forget their journeys and keeps them while they amuse her, seizes hostages or treasures and demands quests or ransoms, sends a lesser fae to pick a fight with travellers and then demands they carry her letters to other faerie nobles as amends, shadowing them with fresh trials. She looks a beautiful olive-skinned woman with moss-grown wooden antlers in wild, flowered hair, amber eyes like frozen sap and a gown of leaves and cobweb, trailing fireflies or snowflakes as the season runs, and nature flourishes where she treads. She can put a man to sleep with a word, turn him into a hare or squirrel until her terms are met, wipe out his memory of home, sway a crowd with her storytelling, and ride the wind as whirling leaves; she bears a glass-bladed dagger that becomes whatever weapon a favoured knight wishes and marks him as hers in her lands, and 10 pawns of Herbam vis lie in her antlers. Iron and the Divine hurt her, and she loses interest in her playthings once they turn fae themselves.

She has sheltered many magi as refugees, vassals or allies, among them Maugris and Dama, who spent long years at her court seeking the mysteries of Story Magic. She claims to hold Cortana. Oberon or the Boar King of Normandy might court or quarrel with her, and some wonder whether Isabella of Angoulême's undying beauty is her gift.

levels.name: The marsh shore
levels.notes: The lowest of six levels: the first touch of the court's paradise over the muddy shore.

levels.name: The heart of the castle
levels.notes: Oriande's court, where her Might rises to 60.

neighbours.name: The Moors of Bazas
neighbours.summary:
Marsh and heath south-west of Bazas, on the edge of the Landes, with a few good stands of pine and oak that the locals cut only now and then. Shepherds watch their flocks from stilts above the fens. Tres and his band hide in this hard country between stays in their sancta: with so many pilgrims about nobody notices a party on the road or camping in the open, and the moors put off all but the most stubborn visitors.

The shepherds tell of a shining white beast at the edges of the woods, which looks out from the trees for a moment and goes back; a sighting means three days' safety for the flock. It is a unicorn (Divine Might 20, Animal): a charger-sized horse with cloven goat's hooves, a beard, a lion's tail and a slender spiral horn, which can tell a virgin by her eyes, wraps itself in white light when roused to righteous fury, cures poison by touch, and is weakened by virgin women. Four pawns of Divine-aligned Animal vis lie in its horn. The Valerenes of Agen seek it eagerly.

neighbours.name: The Caves of Roquetaillade
neighbours.summary: Caves near Roquetaillade Castle by Langon, home to a company of faerie masons. Each new lord de La Motte enlarges the castle with their help, which is how the square four-towered keep has grown so grand.
neighbours.secrets: The masons are bound by a pact to finish one building work for each new lord of the family. Its terms are secret, told only by a dying lord to his son.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Marmande
neighbours.summary:
A walled town on the Garonne that Richard the Lionheart founded around 1195. The count of Toulouse held it by 1209; de Montfort's men took it in 1212 and again in 1213 after a revolt, and it went over to King John when an English army came near in 1214, until the English fell back after Bouvines. Just after Christmas 1218 crusaders of Prince Louis under Centule d'Astarac laid siege; after nine months the garrison yielded and marched out on terms that were kept. Then, on the Bishop of Saintes's word, Amaury de Montfort's men killed all five thousand townsfolk, women and children too, and even the beasts, saying it was needed to keep God's favour on their arms, then burned the town and razed what they could. Many say the young Amaury did it to avenge his father, killed at Toulouse.

In 1220 it is a field of rubble and ash where the charred bones of the dead lie unburied. The Infernal aura is 6, rising to 7 on 26 September, the anniversary, when those with Second Sight see the ground drenched in the slaughter as if it had rained from the sky. Ghosts are common, and so are crows corrupted by feeding on the dead.

neighbours.name: The Mithraea under Auch Cathedral
neighbours.summary: Catacombs beneath the burnt-out cathedral in the middle of Auch, which was raised over several temples of Mithras. Six whole tauroctony altars of white marble stand hidden there, where initiates once purified themselves and were admitted to the mysteries. The altars and the chamber round them hold a Magic aura of 3; the cathedral above, a cleared site with a few stretches of new wall since the fire of 1170, has no Divine aura at all.

neighbours.name: The Lou Carcolh's Cavern
neighbours.summary:
A cave in the hills near Bayonne where the mountains begin, the lair of the Lou Carcolh (Magic Might 25, Animal): a vast snail with a dragon's head, a beard of a score of tentacles that reach a hundred paces to drag prey into a mouth of forearm-long fangs, a lumpy shell and a pebbled hide that turns most blades. It slides over any rubble, feels for prey through the air with its tentacles, and must eat people. It seldom strays far and mostly takes pilgrims, which keeps it fed for now. Five pawns of Animal vis lie in its tentacles.

The sorginak know of it and keep away, but watch it closely; now and then one leads meddling knights, prying magi or foolish bandits to its cave, to feed it and be rid of them. The answers to some questions lie in its lair.

neighbours.name: The Whaling Grounds of Bayonne
neighbours.summary:
The coastal waters off Bayonne and the Basque shore, watched from tall lookout towers, the vigias. When whales, the sarda, are sighted, the whalers launch a fleet of small boats and chase them with harpoons and throwing spears into the shallows. The sarda is a huge, ill-tempered beast with a sweet breath, a pebbled hide and a tail that lies flat, which smashes or overturns boats that harry it.

Whales of Virtue hold Animal vis in their bones and Aquam vis in their baleen; no covenant claims them. Rebecca of Mimizan flies over her home village's boats in albatross form, and the whalers follow her as a lucky sign.

neighbours.name: The Shepherds' Ford at Pau
neighbours.summary:
The crossing of the Gave de Pau below Pau's two square towers, used by shepherds driving flocks to and from the mountain pastures since time out of mind. Tufts of wool caught on the brambles along the drove road yield 4 pawns of Creo vis at the spring equinox and 4 of Muto at the autumn equinox; no covenant holds them.

A covenant might be founded in the towers if it guarded the crossing, kept the village and took fair tolls for the young William of Béarn, who would turn a blind eye to its oddities; but that comes perilously close to serving as court wizards.

neighbours.name: The Healing Spring of Lourdes
neighbours.summary:
A spring in a bend of the Gave de Pau by Lourdes, one of the invigorating baths the Romans prized in Bigorre, said to heal. Its water drawn at the first snowmelt yields 4 pawns of Creo vis, held by no covenant.

On the anniversary of Mirat's baptism the top of the castle tower has a Divine aura of 2. The lord of the castle in 778, the Moor Mirat, held out against Charlemagne until an eagle dropped a great trout at his feet; he threw it down to the besiegers, who took it to mean the castle could hold for ever and left. Bishop Turpin of Le Puy persuaded him that the eagle and the retreat were miracles of the Virgin; Mirat gave gifts to the Black Virgin of Le Puy, yielded the castle, was baptised, and took the name Louerda, the rose, which the town now bears.

neighbours.name: Castra Solis
neighbours.summary:
Limestone hills on the Garonne about halfway between Bordeaux and La Réole, where the domus magna of House Flambeau looks like a rich manor or Roman villa among vineyards and fields that grow neither wine nor wheat: they are tourney grounds for the House's many contests. The Magic aura is only 3.

At the foot of the cliffs a network of riverside caves, inside the Aegis and warded besides, climbs under oyster-crusted arches to a large underground temple, believed by most Flambeau to be Kaeso's Roman mithraeum.

neighbours.name: The Mithraeum of Castra Solis
neighbours.summary: The temple under Castra Solis, reached by hidden stairs from the library to the chambers behind it. Generations of Christian milites and pious magi have given it a Divine aura of 4, and it is a church in all but name: the rites for the Legion of Mithras's younger initiates are close to baptism, communion and the last rites. Tombs in the caves hold fallen milites in holy ground; the former Primus Entisimon lies here, but Kaeso does not.
neighbours.secrets: It is a copy, built when Bordeaux fell to the raiders; the true temple lies under Bordeaux and was kept secret so that its power would endure.

neighbours.name: Dama's Tower at Mimizan
neighbours.summary:
A chapter of Castra Solis: Dama of Merinita's tower on the swampy shore on the north side of the lake outside Mimizan, a squat block of stone three storeys high over a cellar used for storage. Dama lives and works on the top floor, guests lodge on the second and the servants on the first. The Redcaps call it Mimizan covenant, but at Tribunal it counts as part of Castra Solis. It began as one of the Hoplites' outposts in the long war with the raiders, and Dama has kept it since the century after the Schism War; she was born close by.

The Faerie aura is 4, centred on a muddy black rock almost buried at the water's edge, near the ruins of a Gaulish shrine where priests made many sacrifices; the wild coast and marshes round about often hold pockets of Faerie aura. A very strong Aegis of the Hearth (level 50, cast with Wizard's Communion and a casting tablet) guards the tower, and Dama's Veil of Haunting Terror, laid along the game trail that rings the grounds and runs out to the main road, fills anyone without Magic Resistance who sets foot on it with visions of their worst fear and an overwhelming urge to run. The locals fear the marsh and tell ghost stories of the things down that trail. Only a small track from the south-west is left clear, and Redcaps know to use it.

Dama and Rebecca are its only magi, with Rebecca's apprentice Alexa and their servants.
neighbours.secrets:
The black rock is where the Gauls drowned captives for Maju, then worshipped as Teutates; an inscription lies under the mud, and votive silver rings lie in the lake. The site is Infernal now, but Maju keeps the aura cloaked so it seems Faerie, at a constant cost to its Might.

Dama made the place frightening on Maju's advice, saying the Veil protects it from crusaders.

neighbours.name: The Copse of Mimizan
neighbours.summary:
A stand of scrub trees inland from Dama's tower on the north side of the lake, with a Faerie aura of 3. Every year twelve Basque folk witches and some Ex Miscellanea magi meet here with Dama to help her and to plan the coming months; she leads the gathering and initiates many of them into the Matres and Matrones. Nearly all honour her as a grande dame, and a few revere her as a saint.

The sorginak of the Basque covens, at least sixty-one unGifted and about nine Gifted in thirteen covens across the west of the Tribunal and north-west Iberia, trade news, favours, apprentices and vis among themselves and mostly defer to Dama; they also gather at akelarre. Only the Gifted, who have sworn the Oath, belong to the Order. About nine Gifted sorginak live in or near Bayonne in Labourd, others round Pau in Béarn, in Soule and in Pyrenean villages; three Hermetic sorginak who live alone keep out of Dama's circle.

neighbours.name: Marie's Manor near Poitiers
neighbours.summary: A chapter of Castra Solis: Marie of Merinita's manor house near Poitiers in Poitou, which counts as part of the covenant though it stands in lands usually reckoned the Normandy Tribunal's. Marie attends the Provençal Tribunal and is working to push its border north by spreading the language and culture of the south through Aquitaine; since the Tribunal runs wherever Occitan is spoken, the claim may have to be settled with Normandy.

neighbours.name: Henry III, King of England and Duke of Aquitaine
neighbours.summary: The boy king of England, fourteen in 1220, whose crown has held Gascony firmly since Richard the Lionheart. The dukes rule from Bordeaux and leave the rest alone, but for the odd show of force down the Garonne. Henry visits his mother Isabella nearby, likes to lodge at Belin, and has made Archbishop Guillaume Amanieu his Seneschal and Guardian of his lands overseas.

neighbours.name: Hugh X of Lusignan, Count of Angoulême
neighbours.summary: Count of Angoulême by his marriage to Isabella of Angoulême, King John's widow and Henry III's mother, and overlord of Blaye (see The Lion and the Lily). Isabella, wed first at twelve, Eleanor of Aquitaine's choice for John and called Messalina, a siren and the Helen of Gaul by the English, married him without waiting for the English council's leave, which a queen dowager must have; the council seized her dower and stopped her pension, and the pair answered by threatening to keep Henry's ten-year-old sister Joan, promised to Alexander II of Scotland, in France, perhaps at Castle Rudel. She will bear Hugh nine more children and her beauty never fades: faerie blood, a bargain with Oriande la Fée, or a pact with Ducaru of Stella Durus?

neighbours.name: Geoffrey I, Lord of Blaye
neighbours.summary: Castellan of the rich port of Blaye from Castle Rudel, beside the basilica, for the counts of Angoulême. His family has held the post for generations at the counts' pleasure, and Hugh X has lately confirmed him in it.

neighbours.name: The Lord of Blanquefort
neighbours.summary: Keeper of the white limestone castle in the Médoc that guards the Levade and the Channel Soulac, charged with taking the toll from travellers on the road.

neighbours.name: The Baron de La Motte
neighbours.summary: Lord of Roquetaillade near Langon, said to be the first castle Charlemagne built, a square stronghold with four towers that each lord of the line has made grander.
neighbours.secrets: The faerie masons of the nearby caves build for each new lord under a family pact passed from father to son on the deathbed.

neighbours.name: Pierre-Gerald, Count of Armagnac
neighbours.summary: Ruler of Auch on the Gers. He dislikes the crusading archbishop Garsie de Lhort, an old enmity rooted in the crusade: his father, the late count, loved the trobairitz Lombarda, whom he met in Toulouse and wrote to all through the war without their love ever being fulfilled, and died in 1219 before they could meet again; the son blames the archbishop's support of the crusade.

neighbours.name: Centule, Count of Astarac
neighbours.summary: A Gascon count who led Prince Louis's crusaders to the siege of Marmande just after Christmas 1218 and held it nine months, until the garrison surrendered and the town was massacred.

neighbours.name: William Raymond, Count of Béarn
neighbours.summary:
An aged count who governs from Tarbes, leaving Pau to his son William. Béarn lies at the foot of the Pyrenees, caught between the crown of Aragon and the crusade on its doorstep; it is no Cathar stronghold, but the late count helped Toulouse and Foix more than once and its knights have no love for crusaders. William Raymond looks to Aragon; his son leans to the English in Aquitaine. His rights to Pau are contested, since his brother's widow Petronilla of Bigorre married Guy de Montfort.

If the saga follows history, he dies in 1223 and William turns to Aragon and tries to take Cerdagne.

neighbours.name: William of Béarn
neighbours.summary: Heir of Béarn, who holds Pau and its ford for his father and favours the English. He might grant magi the towers above the ford in return for guarding the crossing and taking fair tolls.

neighbours.name: Guy de Montfort, Count of Bigorre
neighbours.summary:
Simon de Montfort's son, count of Bigorre by marriage to Petronilla of Bigorre. He is away with the crusade and Petronilla lives at Poitiers out of reach of reprisals, so Tarbes has no seneschal and its towns keep order as best they can with the bishop and clergy. Bigorre's capital at Lourdes, with its salt valleys, matters more to the crusade than Tarbes.

If the saga follows history, he is killed in April 1220 in a skirmish with the count of Toulouse's men near Castelnaudary.

neighbours.name: The Count of Labourd
neighbours.summary: A Basque lord who has lived at Ustaritz, ten miles east of Bayonne, since Richard the Lionheart crushed the local barons in 1177 for rising against King Henry and held Bayonne himself until 1199. Bayonne's charter of 1215 freed the city from his authority. With Bayonne's trade tied to Cornwall and Aquitaine he has little hope of it back; bitter, he thinks of buying the sorginak's curses to bring the town to heel.

neighbours.name: Bordeaux Cathedral
neighbours.summary:
The archbishop's seat, consecrated by Urban II in 1096. Its archbishops are often open agents of English policy, and Guillaume Amanieu is no exception: Henry III has named him Seneschal and Guardian of all his lands overseas. No meek scholar, he has fought in the Reconquista and the Albigensian Crusade, and quarrels often with Simon de Sully, archbishop of Bourges.

The city's other great churches are the basilicas of St Seurin and of St Michel, the latter outside the walls; Roland's broken horn, the Olifant, is said to rest in St Seurin.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of Sainte-Croix de Bordeaux
neighbours.summary: A powerful Benedictine abbey of Bordeaux, with a small daughter house north-west of Soulac, the first monastery in the area.

neighbours.name: The Church of Belin
neighbours.summary: The tomb church of Olivier de Viennes, Ogier the Dane and other Peers of Charlemagne, Divine aura 4, its air sweet with a healing scent; its Creo vis is described with Belin.

neighbours.name: The Cathedral of St John the Baptist, Bazas
neighbours.summary: The bishop's church of Bazas, where pilgrims on the Limoges road pray before going on to Ostabat. St Veronica built its oratory, and its altar holds a relic of the Baptist's blood that Urban II declared genuine in 1092; he came back in 1096 to preach the Crusade here. Divine aura 5, 6 on 29 August, the feast of the Baptist's beheading.

neighbours.name: The Templar Hospital of Bazas
neighbours.summary: A hospital the Templars keep in Bazas for pilgrims on the Way.

neighbours.name: The Basilica of Saint-Romain, Blaye
neighbours.summary:
A basilica over the Gironde estuary, a favourite stop on the Way: pilgrims pray at its crypt and altar before taking the ferry. In the crypt Charibert, the old king of Aquitaine, and Roland, Charlemagne's greatest paladin, lie in white marble tombs. Divine aura 4, rising to 5 on 15 August, the day Roland died, and on St Romain's day, 24 November. A hospice of St Nicholas beside it cares for pilgrims.

Roland's relic-filled sword Durendal and his horn, the Olifant, carved from a unicorn's horn and split by his last blast, are not here. The horn is said to be in St Seurin at Bordeaux. Durendal's golden hilt is said to hold a tooth of St Peter, blood of St Basil, a lock of St Denis's hair and a scrap of the Virgin's clothing, a mighty weapon against demons and harmful magic; the Confraternity of Roland says it was the work of Wayland Smith and Verditius together. Roland is said to have cut the Brèche de Roland with it and flung it away; a sword stuck in the cliff under the abbey of Rocamadour may be it, unless Charlemagne took it and Roscius of Verditius later stole it away to Verdi.

neighbours.name: The Church of St Martin, Blanquefort
neighbours.summary: A white limestone church whose crypt holds a great marble sarcophagus, perhaps the tomb of one of Charlemagne's Peers.

neighbours.name: Notre-Dame de la Fin des Terres, Soulac
neighbours.summary: The church where many English pilgrims begin the Way, rich in relics: a candle from the Nativity, palm leaves strewn before Christ in Jerusalem, and above all drops of the Virgin's milk. Divine aura 4. The Hospitallers keep a hospice in the town.

neighbours.name: The Cathedral of St Thomas, Auch
neighbours.summary:
The seat of an archdiocese since 879, when it moved from Eauze. The cathedral burned in 1170, and rebuilding has gone no further than clearing the rubble and raising a few stretches of wall; it has no Divine aura. Its relics travel with the archbishop, Garsie de Lhort, since 1214, who usually rides with Prince Louis's crusaders and was at the massacre of Marmande. The count of Armagnac loathes him.

If the saga follows history, nobody tries to rebuild until 1310.

neighbours.name: The Church of Saint Caprasius, Agen
neighbours.summary: Agen's church, where the Valerenes light candles each midsummer before walking to Limoges.

neighbours.name: The Cathedral of St Mary, Bayonne
neighbours.summary: A great cathedral begun in 1213 and still building; its finished crypts hold the relics of the city's patron, Leon de Carentan, whom Vikings beheaded in the ninth century. Divine aura 2, rising to 3 on his feast, 1 March.

neighbours.name: The Bishop's Palace and Cathedral of Tarbes
neighbours.summary: The cathedral and bishop's palace at the heart of Tarbes, ringed by the town's six walled villages; with no seneschal, the bishop and clergy help the towns keep order. Legend says Tharbis, the Cushite queen of Ethiopia whom Moses spurned, founded the town. Two heirlooms pass from bishop to bishop: a polished walking staff of African moringa wood, which the bishop keeps in his office unused, and a plain gold ring set with amber in a soapstone box.
neighbours.secrets: Whoever is given the ring and told to think of a subject slowly forgets it: an Intelligence roll each full moon against 7, plus 1 for each failure, and after five failures it is gone. The effect is not Hermetic (a season and an InMe Lab Total of 30 to work out). The ring holds 4 pawns of Mentem vis and is an Arcane Connection to the spirit of Tharbis. Its power was forgotten when a dying bishop gave it to his successor and told him never to forget it.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of Saint-Savin
neighbours.summary: An abbey and convent south of Lourdes. Roland lodged here while Charlemagne besieged Lourdes and repaid the monks by killing the giants Passamont and Alabaster, who lived near their priory and ate their flocks.
neighbours.secrets: The giants were faeries and did not die: their essence passed into the skull fetishes Roland left behind, and they now dwell deeper in the Pyrenees, behind tales of savage brutes haunting the high pastures and passes.

neighbours.name: The Bessaut Commandery
neighbours.summary: The Order of Santiago's chief house in the Tribunal, with the new hospital of Our Lady Mary Magdalene, built on a gift from Guilhem de Mazerolles in 1219. Eight knights, their households and forty men-at-arms serve here, apart from any town. The Knight Commander, Juan Marcos Correa, is a cheerful veteran of the Reconquista on good terms with the other orders' houses; his brother is also of the Order in Iberia.

neighbours.name: Bordeaux
neighbours.summary: The great port on the Garonne and the stronghold of English power in the region since Eleanor of Aquitaine's marriage to Louis was annulled. It trades briskly in tin and lead from southern England, passing the metal on to France and beyond, and is a major stop on the Way of St James. Cenodoxus Superbia and Julian the Tempter hunt its crowds.
neighbours.ruler: Henry III, as Duke of Aquitaine
neighbours.secrets: Kaeso's true mithraeum lies in a cavern under its southern quarter.

neighbours.name: Blaye
neighbours.summary: An ancient, prosperous port on the Gironde, older than Caesar's conquest and a bulwark of Charlemagne's against the Saracens, where pilgrims take the ferry across the estuary; Julian the Tempter haunts the crossing.

neighbours.name: Soulac
neighbours.summary: A small town at the tip of the Médoc where many English pilgrims start the Way, with a Hospitaller hospice and the basilica of Notre-Dame de la Fin des Terres.

neighbours.name: Langon
neighbours.summary: A trading port on the left bank of the Garonne and a stop on the Way before Bazas, near Roquetaillade Castle.

neighbours.name: Bazas
neighbours.summary: A walled cathedral city on the edge of the Landes where the Garonne meets the Brion, a regular stop on the Limoges road of the Way, with a Templar hospital and the cathedral of St John the Baptist.

neighbours.name: Auch
neighbours.summary: The archbishop's town on the Gers, ruled by the count of Armagnac, with its burnt-out cathedral and the mithraea beneath.

neighbours.name: La Romieu
neighbours.summary: A small village about a mile from the ruins of Nemetannais, a Diedne covenant. The country round it teems with matagots (Magic Might 15, Animal): big dark calico cats flecked with gold, with tufted ears and cruel eyes. A matagot serves whoever first feeds it until that person dies or lets it go, conjures a hidden hoard of coins worth some twenty pounds and pays it out when its family pleases it, and racks with pain anyone who will not release it. Three pawns of Animal vis lie in its tail.

neighbours.name: Bayonne
neighbours.summary: A great shipbuilding and whaling port, rebuilt by Basques and Viking settlers in the mid-tenth century. King John's charter of 1215 gave it a mayor, jurors, councillors and advisers and freed it from the count of Labourd. Its whalers are a skilled, well-ordered community of fine shipwrights and sailors who have hunted the sarda for nearly two hundred years. About nine Gifted sorginak live in and around it; Cenodoxus and Julian prey on its crowds. The ruins of Lapurdum, a Flambeau mithraeum abandoned to the Vikings, lie within the city.

neighbours.name: Ostabat
neighbours.summary: The Basque town where four routes of the Way meet before Roncevaux: two hotels, two hospitals and over two dozen hostels, with more than five thousand palmers a week passing toward the rough stone tunnel into Iberia, inside which an inn shelters travellers and their mounts from storm and snow. Drakes and worms are worst here.

neighbours.name: Pau
neighbours.summary: A town the count of Béarn founded in the eleventh century on the north bank of the Gave de Pau to guard its ford, which two large square towers overlook.

neighbours.name: Tarbes
neighbours.summary: The capital of Bigorre, on the left bank of the Adour: six walled villages round the bishop's palace and cathedral. Its oldest ruins are Roman. With Guy de Montfort at war and no seneschal, the towns and the bishop keep order.

neighbours.name: Lourdes
neighbours.summary: A walled town on the Gave de Pau among caves and quarries, with the old seat of the counts of Bigorre, on Roman footings, on a rock east of it: a great square tower the crusaders think more vital than Tarbes, since it commands the salt mines of the valleys. Nearby Bagnères-de-Bigorre has Roman baths.

neighbours.name: Mimizan
neighbours.summary: A coastal village by a lake in the Landes. Its folk fear the marsh on the lake's north side and the trail into it, and tell ghost stories about what lives there: Dama's tower.

neighbours.name: The Court of Rosefleur
neighbours.summary: Oriande la Fée's court and the Dames Blanches who own her as queen, from the Gironde to the Pyrenees and east to the Camargue: courtly fae, nymphs, sirens, trolls and fauns who live in the Médoc's dolmens and torment pilgrims on the Way.

details.wants: Stories: knights and pilgrims forced into quests, ransoms and errands
details.offers: Shelter for refugees, vassals and allies, as Maugris and Dama had; Oriande's glass dagger to a favoured knight

links.note: Spent long years at the court; once sworn to Oriande

neighbours.name: The Whalers of Bayonne
neighbours.summary: The Basque whalers of Bayonne and its coast, who keep watch from the vigias and hunt the sarda in fleets of small boats with harpoons and spears, second to none at their craft.

details.offers: Whale meat and goods; the bones and baleen of Whales of Virtue hold Animal and Aquam vis

neighbours.name: The Knights Templar in Provence
neighbours.summary:
The largest knightly order, exempt by papal bull from local law and taxes. Its commanderies, each with a commander's house, quarters, pilgrim lodging, farm, mill, chapel and graveyard inside a wall, raise men and money for the Holy Land; six to fifty brother knights, as many sergeants and a chaplain hold each, under a commander elected by the brothers. The Tribunal has a hundred: 27 in the Arelat, 20 in Gascony, 14 in the Narbonnais and 29 in the Toulousain, with ten of Auvergne's seventeen inside its bounds, and none in Andorra or the Pyrenees. Those of Gascony and the Toulousain guard the Way and support the Fifth Crusade and the Reconquista. Montsaunès, fifty miles south-west of Toulouse, oversees St Marcet, Boudrac and smaller houses and holdings across the district.

Grand Master Peter de Montaigu of Auvergne, whose brother Guerrin leads the Hospitallers, holds that the only true crusade is against the Saracens, and the Templars would not join the war on the Cathars; Grand Master Bertrand de Blanchefort had Cathar blood, and his kin in the Razès fought for the Cathars. Houses close to Cathar communities have hidden perfecti for short spells. Of the Tribunal's three masters, Giraud Brochard is master of Aquitaine and Guillaume d'Ailly master of Spain and Provence; the third, over Provence's province and bailiwick, died in 1219, and the post stays empty until 1229 if the saga follows history.

neighbours.name: The Knights Hospitaller in Provence
neighbours.summary: The Order of St John of Jerusalem, strong in Provence, which supports pilgrims on the Way and raises revenue for the Levant. Its chief preceptory at Saint-Gilles near Nîmes runs 53 of its 81 holdings across the Arelat, Gascony, the Narbonnais and the Toulousain; the preceptory of Toulouse runs the other 28. It keeps a hospice at Soulac.

neighbours.name: The Order of Santiago
neighbours.summary: The Knights of St James of the Sword, an Iberian order with only a few houses in Provence, all on the Way and mostly in Gascony, there only to guard and help pilgrims. The chief one is the Bessaut Commandery.
neighbours.ruler: Grand Master Martín Peláez Barragán, in Castile

neighbours.name: The Pyrenees and the Hispanic March
neighbours.summary:
The mountain wall between Provence and Iberia, and the realms that climb it from the south: the kingdoms of Castile and Navarre in the west, the crown of Aragon (the kingdom of Aragon and the county of Barcelona, together called Catalonia) in the centre and east, and tiny Andorra in the middle, the last of Charlemagne's marcher counties. The frontier itself is marked only by iron crosses set on lonely slopes and by the watersheds where the thaw runs off one way or the other. The ruling houses here are knotted together by marriage with each other and with England, Burgundy, Toulouse and Montpellier, and they care as much about the war against the Moors as about the crusade in Provence. The book treats the southern lands only where they touch the mountains.

Hermetically the mountains are the Tribunal's conservative heartland. Aedes Mercurii, the Cult of Mercury's great temple and fortress, leads a bloc that wants no part in the crusade; Bellaquin, a banking covenant in Andorra, dreams of a Catalan Tribunal; and the Criamon of Miniata Sophia study painted caves near Foix. Val-Negra, the first domus magna of House Flambeau, lies lost on Mount Perditu. If the Tribunal ever moves against the crusaders, the Pyrenean covenants may walk out and ask the Grand Tribunal of 1228 for a Tribunal of their own. There are no Templar houses in Andorra or the mountains.

Caves honeycomb the range, many big enough for a covenant, but drakes, worms and now and then a wyvern lair in them, so a new covenant may have to evict a tenant first.

The Basques. Their country covers the western mountains and the Biscay coast, across the Provençal and Iberian Tribunals: Labourd, Lower Navarre and Soule on the French side, Upper Navarre under Castile's shadow, and Álava, Biscay and Gipuzkoa held by Castile. A Basque is one who speaks Euskara, a tongue kin to no other, with its own strange numerals; many also speak Occitan, and some northern Basques feel more Occitan than Basque. They have no kingdom of their own but keep their land, language and customs, own their farms rather than serving lords, and are content. Family names come from the place a house stands. Women own property, hold office and speak in council more than elsewhere, though men lead. Nearly all are Christian, but a quiet pagan minority is let be, and Jews, Muslims and heretics who learn the language are tolerated. They are hardy mountaineers, whalers and cod fishers, lately using the stern rudder, and they crew ships from the Mediterranean to the North Sea.

Basque myth. The old faith is chthonic: Mari, an earth mother of weather and fortune, drives a chariot of storm clouds behind great goats and mates with her consort Sugaar, and both bring storms, droughts and luck good and bad; she lives in a mountain cave whose place changes with the teller, appears as a young woman in red, a burning woman, a tree or a thunderbolt, and takes red beasts' shapes or a black he-goat's. She may be a Magic daimon, a faerie living on worship, or a demon's mask; nobody can be sure. Sugaar is the Great Dragon and the genius loci of the whole range, a serpent up to seven hundred feet long or a black ram, a storm or a warrior, said to have been bound to the mountains by the Archangel Michael. Their brood are the drakes, worms, many-headed herensuge and venomous vibria of the Pyrenees; their son Mikelatz is a wild storm spirit; Atxular, Mari's son by a pious man, turned from black magic to protect Christians and justifies Christian sorginak; and Jaun Zuria, the White Lord, first lord of Biscay, was Sugaar's son.

Other beings. The jentilak, giants who held the land before men, raised the dolmens, taught farming and smithing, and are said to have thrown boulders at Roland; a few linger on the peaks as magical beings or faeries, and one, Olentzero, brings children gifts at Christmas. The one-eyed, man-eating tartalo may be their degenerate kin. The laminak are river fae, builders and spinners, who teach sorginak and raise bridges and churches for a price; whoever steals a lamia's golden comb commands her, and none may tread holy ground. Aker, goat-men of the mountain meadows, are called by sorginak to teach weather lore and herbs or harry enemies, and demons sometimes pose as aker.

The sorginak are Basque folk witches descended from Mari's priestesses (P11: their powers are not modelled). The unGifted live quietly in the villages; the Gifted live apart, some trained as folk witches and some Hermetically, and bully their weaker sisters. At least 61 unGifted and about nine Gifted sorginak meet in 13 covens across western Provence and north-western Iberia, at Friday gatherings called akelarre in caves and stone circles, with grand conclaves at Zugarramurdi. Most defer to Dama, the Praeco, at Mimizan; three Hermetically trained sorginak keep apart from her. Their favoured powers are Animal Ken, Dowsing, Flight, Healing, Hex, Second Sight and Shapeshifting; a warped sorgina of some lines slowly becomes a lamia, wholly so at Warping 10. A covenant in the Basque country will have dealings with a coven, friendly or not.

neighbours.name: The Basque Country and Navarre
neighbours.summary:
The western mountains and their northern valleys. Labourd runs from the Bay of Biscay to Mount Rhune and is the heart of Basque culture, full of sorginak; its count lost Bayonne after rebelling against Henry II. Lower Navarre, a land of hills and valleys that has swung between Gascony and Navarre, now owes Navarre and is run by a royal sheriff with no lord; it lives off the Way of St James, which musters at Ostabat and climbs to Roncevaux, and is known for pink sandstone, wild pottok ponies and the Irouleguy wine of Roncevaux's monks, while its many dolmens hint that jentilak once lived here. Soule, on the Oloron opposite Béarn, speaks Euskara and little else.

South of the passes lies Upper Navarre, whose capital Pamplona grows rich on pilgrims. The Bitter Lord (a story seed): the Count of Labourd thinks of hiring sorginak to curse, frighten and blackmail Bayonne's officers, then offering to lift the trouble in exchange for the town's fealty.

neighbours.name: Mount Rhune
neighbours.summary:
The mountain at Labourd's eastern edge, its slopes strewn with stone circles, dolmens and old burial mounds where the sorginak of Labourd hold their akelarre. It has a Magic aura of 4. A coven from round Ustaritz, the county's capital, flies here as ravens for its Friday sabbat.

Lehen Sugea, a seven-headed, winged, fire-breathing dragon, is said to sleep deep inside the mountain.

neighbours.name: The Cave of Zugarramurdi
neighbours.summary:
A vast cave mouth opening on a broad meadow, with a stream running through the gallery: a gathering place of folk witches since antiquity. Every third year at midsummer sorginak from Normandy, Iberia and Provence meet here for a great conclave of strange rites and initiations, and trade vis and secrets.

Its aura is Magic 4, but vis drawn from it is Infesta, tainted by the Infernal (Realms of Power: the Infernal). No covenant claims it.

neighbours.name: Roncevaux Pass
neighbours.summary:
The pass on the Way of St James where Charlemagne's rearguard was destroyed in 778, with a hostel for pilgrims, the Chapel of Puerto de Ibañeta and a stone where Roland is said to have fallen; the real battlefield is in the Valcarlos below, which Verditius magi visit for their mystery rites. Sancho VII gave the church part of his spoils from Las Navas de Tolosa, among them the great emerald from the sultan's turban, and it keeps Our Lady of Roncevaux, a cedar and silver statue a deer is said to have led the priests to. The Divine aura is 3 over the whole area, and 4 on the battle's anniversary.

The Basques tell the battle as an ambush by lightly armed mountaineers; the Song of Roland makes it four hundred thousand Saracens. Both are told true: the Saracens came with Basque guides and jentil mercenaries. Faeries feed on the tale and draw mortals in to replay it, with Roland facing Moors or a band of Basques as suits the faeries' game.

neighbours.name: The Tower on Mount Urkulu
neighbours.summary: A half-ruined Roman tower on Mount Urkulu, looking north and south and down on the road through Roncevaux; many call it a Mercurian site. The sheriff's garrison keeps watch from it for travellers, but leaves smartly every Friday, when a busy coven of sorginak holds akelarre inside its walls, often calling up a wild aker to teach or serve, or using ecstatic magic to answer questions and pay back insults (a story seed).

neighbours.name: The Caves of Soule
neighbours.summary: Soule's limestone hills, pitted with sinkholes and caverns, house a few drakes and worms said to be Sugaar's offspring, and a great many laminak, who are believed to teach their secrets to the Basque folk witches.

neighbours.name: The Caves of Betharram
neighbours.summary: A cave system on the northern, Toulousain side of the mountains, running nearly three kilometres underground through several big galleries along an underground river: a possible covenant site, if whatever drake or worm lairs there can be put out.

neighbours.name: The High Pyrenees
neighbours.summary: The central range above Béarn and Bigorre, the wildest country in the Tribunal: glaciers and pine forest, the Cirque de Gavarnie, Mount Perditu and the Breach of Roland, and the distinctive peak of Pic du Midi d'Ossau, seen from Pau on a clear day. Aedes Mercurii holds both of its sites here, and Val-Negra lies lost among these peaks.

neighbours.name: Mount Perditu
neighbours.summary:
The highest mountain of the range, clad in pines and glaciers, and named the lost mountain for how far it lies from anywhere. It belongs with the Breach of Roland; its three summits are said to be three sisters whose faith and grief changed them when Visigoths razed their village. Pyrene's ghost (see the Cairn of Pyrene) is sometimes seen at its foot or at the Breach.

Val-Negra, the fallen domus magna of House Flambeau, lies hidden in a regio on its slopes, two miles south of Aedes Mercurii's Templum.

neighbours.name: The Breach of Roland
neighbours.summary:
A notch forty paces wide between cliffs a hundred paces high, in the ridge above the Cirque de Gavarnie, which Roland is said to have cut when he tried to break Durendal as he lay dying, though Roncevaux is over a hundred miles off.

Its aura of 2 is sometimes Magic and sometimes Divine, at random, which hints at something very strange.

neighbours.name: The Cairn of Pyrene
neighbours.summary:
Pyrene's hidden tomb, somewhere deep in the range. The tale: Heracles, a guest at her father's court on his way to steal Geryon's cattle, seduced her in drink; she bore a serpent, fled to tell the trees her grief, and was torn apart by beasts. Heracles came back, heaped stones over what was left of her and commanded the land to keep her name, and the hills piled up stone on stone into the Pyrenees. Magical beasts are said to haunt the place, and the site, Magic 4, joins a network of regiones that runs through the whole range.

Vis: on the night of her death her ghost weeps before the cairn until dawn, and the dew that gathers in a hollow of the boulder where she sits holds 4 pawns of Mentem vis (unclaimed).

Pyrene the Spectre: a ghost of Magic Might 14 (Mentem), a pale, lovely, raven-haired woman in a torn linen dress, her lower legs mangled and her feet bloody, her face streaked with tears. She can turn invisible at will (Second Sight still sees her) and take solid form, calms and commands magical creatures, and knows the passes and the mountains' regio paths. She speaks Euskara, Occitan, Latin and Gothic, is grieving, reclusive and proud, fears daylight, and carries three pawns of Mentem vis in her dress.

Story questions: what does she know of Heracles; what became of the serpent she bore, a vouivre perhaps; and could she be talked into sharing the regio network made when the mountains were born?

neighbours.name: Jaca, Sobrarbe and Ribagorza
neighbours.summary: The mountain counties of the crown of Aragon, ruled by James I's regents until he comes of age. Jaca, also called the county of Aragon, once belonged to Navarre and became the core of the Aragonese kingdom; Sobrarbe and Ribagorza, joined by marriage since the tenth century, have many Basques and a remnant of Muslims living peaceably among the Christians, and Ribagorza holds the highest peaks of the range. South of the mountains.

neighbours.name: The Mallos de Riglos
neighbours.summary:
Near-vertical pillars of sedimentary rock in the foothills, some three hundred paces tall. Six miles east on a limestone bluff stands Castle Loarre, an eleventh-century fortress lately given new outer walls and towers by Pedro II, with its village beneath and a house of Augustinian canons from Montearagón inside.

A Giant Witch (a story seed): the people of Loarre say a jentil sorgina lives among the pillars. She was once the witch of a village called Foz de Escalettes, but as her size showed the villagers fled, and she drew more rock up out of the ground to hide in. Magic auras and vis sources are common round her.

neighbours.name: The Catalan Counties
neighbours.summary:
The eastern Pyrenees under the crown of Aragon. Besalu, joined to Barcelona early in the twelfth century, is thick with monasteries (the nuns of Sant Joan de les Abadesses, Santa María de Ripoll, Bañolas, Camprodón, Sant Pau de Fenollet), and its northern castles of Tautavel, Vingrau, Queribus and Aguilar guard remote passes and now shelter Cathar refugees. Conflent, the Têt valley, is Nuno Sanche's, with strong castles and the fortified town of Villefranche-de-Conflent, under Mount Canigou.

Cerdagne, also Nuno Sanche's, is still scarred by Raymond Roger of Foix's raids of 1195 to 1203, when he burned churches and attacked monasteries pressing his claim to Andorra; the crusade cut the recovery short, and most Divine auras here are fading remnants. Its Segre valley, the only one in the range that runs east to west, gets the sun and good harvests. Pallars is remote and snowbound in winter, all but ungoverned. Urgell is ruled from La Seu d'Urgell by the dying Countess Elvira.

Contested County (a story seed): the Count of Ager claims Aurembiaix cannot inherit Urgell; if history runs its course he seizes the county in the winter of 1220 and she flees, a possible companion or patron. In 1228 James I has her marriage annulled, takes her as his mistress and confirms her rights for the town of Lleida. Several counties of Roussillon belong to the same lords and are told of with the Narbonnais.

neighbours.name: Mount Canigou
neighbours.summary: The mountain filling Conflent's northern sky, with the abbeys of Saint-Martin-du-Canigou and Saint-Michel-de-Cuxa high on its flanks.

neighbours.name: The Valleys of Pallars
neighbours.summary: Looking for a Lord (a story seed): a covenant in one of Pallars's many valleys or ruined keeps would be left alone for a good while, the land being remote and its count away at the crusade. That lasts until Roger II succeeds in 1234 and takes a close interest in the county and anyone governing it; meanwhile the covenant may have to compete for vis with the Basque sorginak or Dama's cult.

neighbours.name: The Gorges de Galamus
neighbours.summary:
A stark, high-walled canyon where the Agly squeezes through the foothills, two days from Perpignan, with the hermitage of St Anthony clinging to its walls since at least the seventh century. The hermitage has a Divine aura of 2.

At the entrance an old stone bears the word square SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS, which some read as a line about the ploughman and the seed, and others as a charm to put out fire without water.

neighbours.name: The Magdalene's Pool
neighbours.summary: A pool deep in a cave below the hermitage, fed by a spring dedicated to Mary Magdalene, with a Magic aura of 3; it is said to heal.

neighbours.name: Andorra
neighbours.summary:
The last of Charlemagne's Pyrenean marches: five parishes (Canillo, Encamp, Ordino, La Massana and Sant Julià de Lòria), each a handful of mountain villages, about three thousand souls in all. No lord lives here; the Andorrans claim a charter from Charlemagne making them sovereign for their service against the Moors. The Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix both claim the land, neither can enforce it, and the Andorrans ignore them or set one against the other; the heaviest tribute anyone recalls was a present of hams and local produce.

Small as it is, Andorra prospers, selling livestock, wool and a fine mountain wine on both sides of the range, and its rivers carry a modest trade route between Toulouse and Catalonia that keeps it independent but not cut off. Wealthy pilgrims linger for the scenery before going on west. Every Andorran, rich landowner or hired hand, counts himself his own sovereign.

neighbours.name: Ordino
neighbours.summary: The parish and village of Ordino in Andorra, where Bellaquin's large house stands in a pocket of Magic aura 3 among the villagers' homes; the covenant's fortified manor lies at the edge of town where a road climbs the mountain that overlooks most of Andorra. Bellaquin's grogs join the local militia's patrols.

neighbours.name: The Cave of Niaux
neighbours.summary: A cave system in the hidden Vicdessos valley, about a day's ride south of Foix and a little north of Castle Miglos and the village of Niaux: three kilometres of galleries, formations and grottos, and above all paintings older than the Flood. The main gallery is covered with horses, oxen, bison, antelope and handprints, and more are scattered down the passages. The cave has a Magic aura of 4, the main gallery 5. Miniata Sophia lives here; the Redcaps record its site as the village of Niaux.

levels.name: The cave of the first painters
levels.enter: By magic at the new moon, equinoxes and solstices; by drumming or painting by firelight at a solstice
levels.notes: The book gives no aura; the main gallery's 5 is assumed.

neighbours.secrets: A regio lies in the cave, easily entered by magic at the new moon, the equinoxes and the solstices: an ancient magical form of the cave where shamans from before the Flood dance, drum and paint new pictures on the walls. The only way to stumble in is to drum or paint on the walls by firelight at a solstice. The Criamon go there for the last initiation of the Avenue of Adulation.

neighbours.name: Aedes Mercurii: the Dorsum (Pic du Midi d'Ossau)
neighbours.summary:
Aedes Mercurii's better-known site, carved into the summit of Pic du Midi d'Ossau, about ninety kilometres north-west of Val-Negra. It began in the early 900s as a garrison for Val-Negra's wars and has been enlarged ever since into a huge fortress of towers, domes and rotundas hollowed from the rock. Outside it is grim, reached by a narrow track winding along the chasms; inside its maze of halls clashes in every style, since each newcomer builds on. Nobody living there knows all it holds, and many labs and sanctums lie untouched since their owners died or passed into Twilight. The whole mountain has a Magic aura of 5.

It is called the Dorsum, the back of the temple, because the Templum is usually reached from here through a great Mercere Portal in an archway between two courtyards. Deep inside smoulders one of the forges of Hephaestus, kept by the priest of Vulcan.

neighbours.name: Aedes Mercurii: the Templum (Cirque de Gavarnie)
neighbours.summary:
Aedes Mercurii's second site, a chapter of the covenant: plain low buildings round a majestic stone temple in the middle of the Cirque de Gavarnie, about two miles north of Val-Negra. The Temple of Mercury looks older than Christ; some say the old Order of Mercury built it, others that Priamitus and the Cult of Mercury's founders made it look ancient. It is three hundred feet long, ringed with carved columns, beautiful within, with old ancient altars all round, and its holy of holies lies eastward.

The Magic aura is 4 across the Cirque and the outbuildings and 8 inside the temple itself. It is joined to the Dorsum by a Mercere Portal.

neighbours.name: King of Castile
neighbours.summary:
Ferdinand III, son of the King of León, has held Castile since 1217, when his mother gave it up to him after her young brother Henry I, thirteen, was killed by a falling roof tile. Henry's father Alfonso VIII, a champion of the Reconquista and founder of the Order of Santiago, took Álava, Gipuzkoa and Biscay from Navarre by force while Sancho VII was in Africa seeking Almohad help. Ferdinand claims overlordship of Navarre, which renewed its vassalage and joined Castile, Aragon and Portugal against the last Almohads. South of the mountains.

The arms are Castile's castle, drawn as a tower.

neighbours.name: King of Navarre
neighbours.summary: Sancho VII has lived retired in the monastery of Tudela since his victory at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212). He is Richard the Lionheart's brother-in-law (Richard married his sister Berengaria, the queen of England who never saw England) and kept good terms with King John; Alfonso VIII of Castile was at once his cousin, his brother-in-law and by turns his foe and ally. His sister, the regent Blanca, minds the war in the south, and his brother Ramiro, Bishop of Pamplona, wields most authority in the capital. The crown holds Lower Navarre through a sheriff.

neighbours.name: Sheriff of Lower Navarre
neighbours.summary: Lower Navarre has no lord of its own: a royal sheriff collects the taxes and keeps the king's law in its towns and hamlets, and his garrison watches the Roncevaux road from the tower on Mount Urkulu, except on Fridays.

neighbours.name: Lord of Biscay
neighbours.summary: Diego López led the vanguard at Las Navas eight years ago and, with his kin, claims descent from Jaun Zuria, the White Lord, first lord of Biscay, whose true father was the dragon Sugaar in human shape. The dragon's blood may run on in the line as Mythic Blood, Magic Blood or Blood of Heroes. Castile annexed Biscay, Álava and Gipuzkoa in 1200.

neighbours.name: Viscount of Soule
neighbours.summary: Ramon Guillem IV, viscount since 1217, rules the Basque viscounty between the Oloron (the border with Béarn), Lower Navarre and the valleys of Barétous and Salazar, from Mauléon.

neighbours.name: King of Aragon and Count of Barcelona
neighbours.summary: The crown of Aragon unites the kingdom of Aragon and the county of Barcelona. Pedro II the Catholic, husband of Marie of Montpellier, died fighting Simon de Montfort at Muret in 1213, and his son James I, twelve, lives at Zaragoza. His great-uncle Sancho of Barcelona, Count of Roussillon and Cerdagne, and Sancho's son Nuno Sanche, who holds Conflent, Cerdagne, Vallespir and Roussillon, are regents (both described with the Narbonnais). Loyal nobles plan to marry James to Eleanor, daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile, on his thirteenth birthday in 1221, to steady the realm until he comes of age in 1223. The crown claims Jaca, Sobrarbe and Ribagorza, Besalu, Urgell and Pallars.

neighbours.name: Count of Pallars
neighbours.summary: Roger I, brother of the Count of Comminges, married the countess in 1217; she cares only for scripture and not at all for ruling, and he is away fighting the Cathars with the crusade, so Pallars goes almost ungoverned. His son Roger II succeeds in 1234 and is far more watchful.

neighbours.name: Countess of Urgell
