neighbours.summary: Ermengol VIII, who fought off Foix's raids from 1195 and captured Raymond Roger in 1203, died in 1208. His widow Elvira rules from La Seu d'Urgell, but she is ill and not expected to see out the winter of 1220, and she is hastily preparing their daughter Aurembiaix to succeed her, having married her in 1212 to the Castilian noble Álvaro Pérez de Castro to strengthen her claim.

neighbours.name: Count of Ager
neighbours.summary: Urgell's cousin, who says Aurembiaix cannot inherit and threatens to take the county by force when the countess dies; if history is followed he seizes it in the winter of 1220.

neighbours.name: Viscount of Miglos
neighbours.summary: Arnaud de Miglos, the local viscount and a vassal of Foix, keeps a garrison in his castle a little south of Niaux and protects the village, whose people pay their taxes on time and so draw none of his attention to Miniata Sophia.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Urgell
neighbours.summary: His parishes stretch across Cerdagne, Pallars and Urgell, and he claims Andorra, as the Count of Foix does, though neither can make the Andorrans obey. Foix's raids from 1195 burned many of his churches; in 1203 the bishop was handed the captured count and passed him on to Pedro II.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Pamplona
neighbours.summary: Ramiro, brother of Sancho VII, holds most real authority in Pamplona while the king lives retired at Tudela. Pamplona and Urgell are the Basques' two sees.

neighbours.name: Santa María de Ripoll
neighbours.summary: The religious heart of Catalonia, burial place of the counts of Barcelona and Besalu since the ninth century, and a famous seat of learning with over four hundred manuscripts. It rules the abbeys of Saint-Martin-du-Canigou and Montserrat in Conflent. Its carved portal shows, in seven bands, God enthroned in Heaven and scenes of Moses, of David and Solomon, of Jonah and of Cain and Abel. Divine aura 4.

neighbours.name: Sant Joan de les Abadesses
neighbours.summary: A monastery of women in the county of Besalu.

neighbours.name: The Abbeys of Canigou
neighbours.summary: Saint-Martin-du-Canigou, a daughter of Ripoll, and Saint-Michel-de-Cuxa stand high on the slopes of Mount Canigou above Conflent.

neighbours.name: San Salvador de Leyre
neighbours.summary: A Cistercian house near Pamplona, famed for its old abbot St Virila, already renowned by 920, who sat rapt for three hundred years listening to a nightingale to understand eternity, and woke unaged, unaware the time had passed. A Timeless Monk (a story seed): might he have been an early pious magus, and what might his relics in the crypt reveal?

neighbours.name: The Abbey of Roncevaux
neighbours.summary: The monks of Roncevaux keep the pass's chapel and hostel and make the Irouleguy wine of Lower Navarre. Their church holds the sultan's emerald from Las Navas and the cedar and silver statue of Our Lady of Roncevaux.

neighbours.name: The Canons of Loarre
neighbours.summary: Augustinian canons from Montearagón who have served inside Castle Loarre since Pedro I granted them the right.

neighbours.name: Pamplona
neighbours.summary: Navarre's capital on the right bank of the Arga, rich from the pilgrims of the Way of St James coming down from the Tunnel Way and Roncevaux, whom its people are proud to help on to Compostela. Centuries of war have made it something of a fortress, high-walled, where folk speak slowly and mind their own business. Many Basques and Occitan settlers live here, and wandering trobairitz in the Provençal style are much liked. The Romans kept a garrison here, Pompaelo. South of the mountains.

neighbours.name: Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port
neighbours.summary: A town at the foot of the Roncevaux road, razed by Richard the Lionheart in 1177 in a war that also destroyed Aedes Mercurii's large outpost here, whose covenfolk the townsfolk already suspected of witchcraft. Some Hermetic historians think a lapis mercurius once stood in a Mercurian temple in the town, now lost.

neighbours.name: Mauléon
neighbours.summary: Capital of the viscounty of Soule.

neighbours.name: Zaragoza
neighbours.summary: The political heart of Aragon, where the boy king James I lives. Charlemagne's failed siege of it in 778 sent him back over the Pyrenees to Roncevaux. South of the mountains.

neighbours.name: Villefranche-de-Conflent
neighbours.summary: A heavily fortified eleventh-century town where the Têt meets the Cady, the seat of Conflent's government.

neighbours.name: La Seu d'Urgell
neighbours.summary: The see of the Bishop of Urgell and the seat of the county.

neighbours.name: Andorra la Vella
neighbours.summary: The town where the five Andorran parishes send representatives once a year to settle the affairs of the land; the population given is all Andorra's.

neighbours.name: Niaux
neighbours.summary: A village of the Vicdessos valley below Castle Miglos that supplies Miniata Sophia, mostly at second hand, and hosts one of its magi each season as a leper-robed guest; its children call Hans Grandfather. It pays its taxes promptly and draws no attention.

neighbours.name: The Parishes of Andorra
neighbours.summary: The five parishes of Andorra, whose representatives meet yearly at Andorra la Vella. They play the bishop and the count against each other, sell over both sides of the range, and take Bellaquin for a helpful company of rich foreigners.

details.rules: No lords and no vassals: each Andorran is his own sovereign
details.wants: To stay free of the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix
details.offers: Livestock, wool, mountain wine and a quiet road between Toulouse and Catalonia

neighbours.name: The Andorra Company
neighbours.summary: Robert Vasquez's company of elite almogavars, raised in Iberia and France and gathered at Bellaquin as its turb. Their old captain was eaten by a mountain drake on a vis hunt three years ago, and Michael, Robert's unGifted son, thirty, who served as his secretary and protégé, has led them since and made them a disciplined force. Robert means to give each a lesser enchanted device for protection, stamina or keener senses.
neighbours.ruler: Captain Michael, son of Robert Vasquez

details.rules: Robert Vasquez is overall commander, Artemis second in command
details.offers: About eighteen disciplined almogavars, two of them sergeants

neighbours.name: The Sorginak Covens
neighbours.summary:
Thirteen covens of Basque folk witches in western Provence and north-western Iberia, at least 61 unGifted and about nine Gifted, who trade news, favours, apprentices and vis among themselves. Some nine live in or near Bayonne, others round Pau in Béarn, in Soule and in mountain villages, and many more south of the mountains. Only the Gifted, who have all sworn the Oath, count as members of the Order, and most of the Tribunal treats them as eremites; nearly all defer to Dama at Mimizan. They meet at least one Friday a month, the keenest every week, and the Gifted pagans bully the pious and unGifted into attending.

Their power has faded since Charlemagne, under Christianity, rival hedge wizards (Suevi sorcerers, Visigoth artificers, Moorish sahirs) and the Order. The Diedne took sorginak into their House, which split the covens; the first sorginak joined Ex Miscellanea in 955, and some changed House in the Schism War to prove loyalty. Power, Unorganized (a story seed): a Tytalus or Trianoma wanting to break the big covenants' hold on the Tribunal might court the sorginak as a voting bloc.

details.rules: Friday akelarre in caves and stone circles; feuds among sorginak are sorginak business
details.wants: Their auras and vis kept from Hermetic hands; deference to Dama
details.offers: Healing, hexes, flight, shapechanging, second sight; vis and secrets traded at Zugarramurdi

neighbours.name: The Hermetic Sorginak
neighbours.summary: Three Gifted sorginak trained in Hermetic magic, each living alone, who refuse Dama's cult of personality and form a faction of their own (chapter three counts four Ex Miscellanea sorginak eremites). Their tradition descends from a coven that worked with two Bonisagus brothers to fit sorginak powers into Hermetic theory; most were killed soon after by drakes Moorish sahirs lured to their covenant, so few remain. They look down on other sorginak, and their rivalries can turn deadly.

details.wants: To guard their secrets and stand apart from Dama's cult

neighbours.name: The Crestias
neighbours.summary: An outcast people among the Basques, speaking Euskara and sharing most customs, but marked by their looks and a few odd ways. They may own no weapons, horses or dogs, marry only each other, live apart on the poorest land, and enter church by their own door to screened pews. Nobody remembers why. Most are Christian, with more pagans and old superstitions than other Basques. At akelarre they are revered rather than scorned, and said to be stronger in dark magic.
neighbours.secrets: Basque slang calls them not of the people, which may mean the leftovers of some invader, or that they are not wholly human.

neighbours.name: Narbonnais
neighbours.summary:
The Mediterranean lowland the Romans called Gallia Narbonensis and later ages Septimania, between the Rhône, the Massif Central and the eastern Pyrenees. Rome's heirs have lived here for more than a thousand years: Hannibal marched through on his way to Italy, the legions set out from here to conquer Gaul, and Charlemagne's Franks stopped the Moors on this ground. It is a patchwork of vineyards, olive groves, sheep pasture, cork woods and old Roman towns, crossed by the Via Domitia.

In 1220 two men decide its mundane affairs: Raimond VI, count of Toulouse, whose vassals hold Béziers, Narbonne, Nîmes and Rodez, and the boy-king James of Aragon, whose crown holds Gévaudan, Millau, Montpellier and Roussillon and whose vassal rules Foix. Simon de Montfort counted for as much until he fell in 1218, and the Albigensian Crusade has not finished remaking the land; the kings of France watch it closely.

Two living covenants keep to themselves here: Stella Durus on the edge of Narbonne and Ara Maxima Nova among the vineyards outside Perpignan. The ruins of Himinis' Forge and Uxellodunum lie in the region, and two Diedne covenants once stood somewhere in the Massif Central, their names and sites now forgotten.

Rodez is the heart of the troubadours' art, and singers of every rank, from counts to commoners, wander the roads; Narbonne keeps the memory of Viscountess Ermengarde's judgements of love. Jewish scholars teach at Narbonne and Montpellier, notaries draw up the contracts of the consular towns, and Moorish corsairs prey on the coast. Pilgrims cross the land on the Way of St. James, guarded by the Templars and the knights of Aubrac.

neighbours.name: County of Lodève
neighbours.summary: A county of the Aude river country under the counts of Toulouse, given over to vines and flocks of sheep; its Corbières hills are the Pyrenees' first, lowest foothills. Its chief town, Lodève, is a favourite halt on the pilgrims' road to Compostela, and a day's ride north of it the Knights Templar keep a walled and fortified town of their own.

neighbours.name: Lodève
neighbours.summary: A small town on the Way of St. James, busy with pilgrims, in a land of vineyards and sheep. Its cathedral is its pride.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St. Genesius, Lodève
neighbours.summary: The cathedral of Lodève, dedicated to Genesius, a clerk of Arles beheaded in 303 in Diocletian's persecution and now the patron of clerks and notaries; the keystone of the apse shows his martyrdom. Bishop Fulcran, who died in 1006 and is venerated as a saint for the purity of his life, lies incorrupt in its catacombs. Divine aura 5.

relics.name: The incorrupt body of Bishop Fulcran

neighbours.name: The Great Dolmen of Grandmont
neighbours.summary: The largest of the dolmens in the oak wood round the priory of St. Michel de Grandmont, among Roman ruins and lesser standing stones on a high hill above the Lodève country. The priory's Divine aura of 4 rules the hilltop all year, but on the night of the summer solstice a Faerie aura of 4 rises round this one stone; the aura given here is that night's.

neighbours.name: Priory of St. Michel de Grandmont
neighbours.summary: A Grandmontine house, keeping the Rule of St. Stephen, a few miles outside Lodève on a tall hill wrapped in an oak forest full of dolmens and Roman remains. It gives shelter to pilgrims on the road to Compostela. Divine aura 4; on midsummer night the great dolmen in its grounds carries a Faerie aura of 4.

neighbours.name: The Bridge of St. Thibery
neighbours.summary:
The Via Domitia crosses the Hérault at the town of St. Thibery on a segmented stone bridge some 450 feet long. It passes for Roman work, but its spans do not match how the Empire built, and locals wonder whether a faerie or a demon raised it.

A frail old peasant haunts it, bent under a bundle of firewood, leaning on a cane and carrying a lantern. He points out to travellers a split strongbox spilling gold and silver into what looks like calm, deep, clear water below the bridge, offers to mind their goods while they dive for it, and asks only half of what they bring up.
neighbours.secrets:
The old man is the Tempter of St. Thibery, a demon of greed (Infernal Might 15, Vim; Hierarchy 0; a tempter). He is the demon of Greed among the Six Deadly Spirits that came to Gascony with the interdict of 1208, moved here from there. The treasure is his phantasm (Trove Just Beyond Reach, CrIm 20); once the dupe leaps, he turns the river into a churning undertow (Rushing Wages of Greed, ReAq 40, Swim rolls at -6 or drown). He can also take or drop a body, change shape (often a raven), impose an Obsession of Greed, and send dreams of desperate poverty that cost a long-term Fatigue level unless the dreamer makes a Brave roll against 9. He is greedy, selfish, tricky and cowardly; he fights with his stick if he must (Attack +6, Damage +6, Defense +7, Init +4; Soak +2).

Weakness: he can do nothing else until he has counted every coin thrown on the ground and put it in his purse. The purse holds 3 pawns of Vim vis.

neighbours.name: The Ancient Wine Press
neighbours.summary:
A great rectangular trough hewn from the living rock beside a vineyard near St. Thibery, older than anyone remembers. Long ago a mob came upon village girls there at the end of the vintage, took what they saw for a pagan rite, and stoned them all, deaf to their pleas.

Vis (unclaimed): if the first harvest's grapes are trodden here barefoot, the pomace (the seeds, skins and stalks left from the must) holds 4 pawns of Herbam. Treading the last harvest the same way yields 6 pawns, but of vis Infesta.
neighbours.secrets: The girls had been pressing the last grapes when fauns seduced them, and the crowd caught them just after; the taint on the last harvest's vis is that killing.

neighbours.name: County of Béziers
neighbours.summary: Temperate, wooded, rolling country that the house of Carcassonne, the Trencavel, has held since 1034. From 1194 Raimond-Rogier Trencavel ruled it with Carcassonne, Albi and the Razès, owing homage both to Peter II of Aragon and to Raimond VI of Toulouse, until the crusaders took him and he died their prisoner in 1209. The crusaders still hold his lands.

neighbours.name: The Massacre Ground of Béziers
neighbours.summary: The burnt city of Béziers, where the crusaders slaughtered the people in 1209, even those who fled into the churches. The whole city lies under an Infernal aura of 7, which climbs to 8 each 22nd of July, the day of the killing, and fades to nothing through Advent and Lent. It was from the steps of the Madeleine that the legate Arnaud Amaury is said to have told the knights to kill everyone and leave God to sort out his own.

neighbours.name: Béziers
neighbours.summary: A colony Augustus founded for retired legionaries, ringed on three sides by the Orb, whose walls were built from the stone of its own amphitheatre. It sells white wine. As a Cathar stronghold it was all but burnt to the ground by the crusade; rebuilding began in 1215 and has far to go, and the new cathedral rises on the footings of the old one of 1130. Hardly anything else stands: the tall limestone church of the Madeleine, once the viscount's chapel, and the church of St. Aphrodise, the city's first evangelist, built over a third-century burial ground.
neighbours.ruler: The crusaders, against the Trencavel claim

neighbours.name: Church of the Madeleine, Béziers
neighbours.summary: A tall limestone church, formerly the viscount's chapel, one of the few buildings of Béziers left standing; the massacre's Infernal aura smothers it. The church of St. Aphrodise, over a third-century necropolis, also survives.

neighbours.name: Narbonne and the Lower Aude
neighbours.summary: The country round Narbonne and the lower Aude, with the port and fisheries of the city and the old abbey lands of Lagrasse two days to the west. The ducal title, once the counts of Toulouse's, was taken from Raimond VI in the crusade.

neighbours.name: Duchy of Narbonne
neighbours.summary: The ducal title over the region, once held by the counts of Toulouse as their right. Raimond VI lost it in the crusade, and since Simon de Montfort's death in 1218 it has belonged to Arnaud Amaury, archbishop of Narbonne, papal legate and the abbot who led the crusade at Béziers. It is quite separate from the viscounty, which rules the city itself.
neighbours.ruler: Arnaud Amaury, archbishop of Narbonne and papal legate

neighbours.name: Viscounty of Narbonne
neighbours.summary: The secular lordship of the city of Narbonne, distinct from the duchy. The viscounts and the archbishops fought over the city for decades of the last century; now the viscount holds its eastern half and the commune, the bourg. Viscountess Ermengarde, who ruled from 1132 to 1194, is the most famous of the line; in 1115 Viscount Aimery II gave the village of Le Lac to Lagrasse to settle a quarrel with the archbishop.

neighbours.name: Narbonne
neighbours.summary:
A tolerant old city that has been capital of Visigothic Septimania and a possession of the Emirate of Cordoba, where the Via Domitia meets the Via Aquitania. It has a busy port and fishing fleet on the Aude, is a centre of troubadour song, and its well-known Jewish scholars keep several schools. The Via Domitia enters it over a bridge of seven arches.

The archbishop rules its western half and the viscount the east and the bourg. Their long feud has let many churches decay, the cathedral of St. Just and St. Pasteur among them, so the city's Divine aura is only 2, rising to 3 on its patron saints' feasts; the basilica of St. Paul-Serge keeps an aura of 5 always.

Stella Durus stands on the left bank of the Aude just outside the city.
neighbours.ruler: The viscount (east and bourg) and the archbishop (west)

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St. Just and St. Pasteur, Narbonne
neighbours.summary: The archbishop's cathedral, neglected into ruin through the long quarrel between archbishops and viscounts over the city. Its archbishop, Arnaud Amaury, is also papal legate and, since 1218, duke of Narbonne, holding the city's western half.

neighbours.name: Basilica of St. Paul-Serge, Narbonne
neighbours.summary: A basilica raised over a fourth-century cemetery that Constantine founded. Unlike the city's neglected churches, it keeps an unfailing Divine aura of 5.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Mary of Lagrasse
neighbours.summary: A Benedictine abbey some two days' ride west of Narbonne. Nimphridius, abbot of Narbonne, gathered its monks in the seventh century; it became an abbey in 779 and grew rich on Charlemagne's patronage and the gifts of local lords, piling up lands, castles and priories. In the last century it ruled wide lands spread over the Béziers and Toulouse dioceses and Urgell county. It still carries weight in the region, but the crusade has cost it dearly.

neighbours.name: Ermengarde's Courts of Love
neighbours.summary: A mundane custom, not a Hermetic one. Viscountess Ermengarde, who ruled Narbonne from 1132 to 1194, gave five of the judgements of love that André le Chapelain records in his treatise on courtly love, De Arte Honeste Amandi. She wrote to and encouraged many troubadours, and the tradition of song and courtly debate she fostered in Narbonne has outlived her and survived the crusade. Jean Marie of Stella Durus is drawn to it and dreams of a league of troubadour-loving magi.

details.rules: Courtly love judged by a lady's verdict, after the fashion of André le Chapelain's treatise
details.wants: Troubadour song and courtly manners kept alive in Narbonne

neighbours.name: County of Nîmes
neighbours.summary: The eastern march of the counts of Toulouse, theirs by inheritance since the ninth century: rolling hills, streams and woods under a mild Mediterranean sky, rich in cork, grapes and olives. In the hills between Millau and Nîmes lie the Bramabiau gorge and the Grotto of Faeries.

neighbours.name: Viscount of Nîmes
neighbours.summary: A hereditary holding of the counts of Toulouse, the eastern edge of their lands. The viscount who governs Nîmes for the count keeps an order of knights, the Knights of the Arena, in the old amphitheatre.
neighbours.ruler: The viscount of Nîmes, for Raimond VI of Toulouse

neighbours.name: The Arena of Nîmes
neighbours.summary: The Roman amphitheatre of Nîmes, big enough for sixteen thousand, now the seat of the city's government and its refuge in danger; the viscount's knights and the bishop's palace live in apartments built into it. Divine aura 3.
neighbours.secrets: Legend says tunnels under the arena run all the way to the amphitheatre of Arles, which has also been made a fortress.

neighbours.name: Nîmes
neighbours.summary:
A cloth-making city that some say Nemausios, son of Heracles, founded beside a healing spring. Its government sits in the Roman arena. The Tour Magne, an eight-sided tower three storeys and nearly twenty paces high, crowns its highest point and takes in the last of the Roman walls; the Maison Carrée, a perfect Roman temple, houses the four consuls who speak for the city.

Notaries hold office for the county of Nîmes.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Nîmes
neighbours.summary: The bishop's palace stands inside the converted arena, and the see's presence has steadily weakened the old spirit of the Nemausian Spring nearby.

neighbours.name: The Knights of the Arena
neighbours.summary: An order of knights in the service of the viscount of Nîmes, quartered in the apartments of the Roman amphitheatre with the bishop's household.

neighbours.name: The Maison Carrée
neighbours.summary: A Roman temple in the heart of Nîmes, raised on a podium with six columns bearing a portico at each end. It was Apollo's, and judges met there; now the four consuls keep their offices in it. A faint Faerie aura of 1 clings to a hollow of the building, rising to 3 on the 9th of February, the old date of Apollo's festival.

neighbours.name: The Bramabiau Gorge
neighbours.summary: In the hills between Millau and Nîmes the river Bonheur plunges into a cave in a cliff, runs underground through a gorge with six waterfalls, and bursts out of a second cave as the Bramabiau, the Roaring Ox in Occitan, to run down a box canyon toward the sea. From the lower cave the passages can be explored. In a side tunnel just past one waterfall are ancient fetishes and wall paintings that a magus might study for Insight into the cultic Fertility Magic of Ancient Magic. The aura in that passage is Magic 3, rising to 4 under a full moon.

neighbours.name: The Grotto of Faeries
neighbours.summary: A deep cavern south of the Bramabiau, still in the hills between Millau and Nîmes, with an underground river running through its back. Its great galleries, which the locals call cathedrals, drop nearly two hundred paces into the rock and take a hard climb to reach the floor. A band of lesser nymphs (Realms of Power: Faerie) dances and sings there to the river's genius loci, and their voices are the rushing-water sound people hear at the cave mouth. The caves carry Faerie aura 3 throughout.

neighbours.name: The Nemausian Spring
neighbours.summary: A spring near Nîmes. Some say the Gauls made it a shrine to Heracles' son before Caesar came; others that it is the old altar of Volcae, a magic spirit the native tribes worshipped until Rome arrived. A spirit still dwells here, much weakened by the spreading Dominion and the bishop's seat in the arena close by. Vis (unclaimed): every summer solstice it wells up in tiny, very clear pools of steaming water holding 3 pawns of Creo or Aquam.

neighbours.name: County of Rodez
neighbours.summary: Carved out of the old county of Rouergue, first an appanage of Toulouse until the viscount's ancestor seized it in 1112. It is the heart of the troubadours' country. The Templars have held five places here since the mid-twelfth century, sold to them to pay for the count of Toulouse's part in the First Crusade.

neighbours.name: Henry I, count of Rodez
neighbours.summary:
Head of the House of Millau, which has ruled Rodez without a break since 1112, and a troubadour himself, as was his father Hugh II, patron of the abbey of Bonnecombe; he came to the title after his half-brothers Hugh and William, neither long-lived. He is raising his children to love song as he does.

Henry means to take the cross and go on crusade, leaving his eight-year-old son Hugh in the care of the boy's mother, Algayette, heiress of Guy, lord of Scorailles.
neighbours.ruler: Henry I of the House of Millau

neighbours.name: Rodez
neighbours.summary: A farming and market town where the Aveyron meets the Auterne on the Ségala plateau, split into quarters by great double walls because its bishops and counts have long quarrelled over it. The red sandstone west wall of the cathedral, built in 1000 with two towers, is part of the town's defences. The bishop's palace has a tall tower.
neighbours.ruler: The count and the bishop, each behind his own wall

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Rodez
neighbours.summary: A red sandstone cathedral whose west front, with its two towers, doubles as part of the town wall. The bishops are often at odds with the counts. Divine aura 5.

neighbours.name: Church of St. Amand, Rodez
neighbours.summary: A church whose choir is hung with sixth-century tapestries of the miracles of St. Amand, the patron of brewers. Divine aura 4.

neighbours.name: Templar Commanderies of the Larzac
neighbours.summary: The Templars' houses in the county of Rodez: the commanderies of Viala du Pas de Jaux and Sainte-Eulalie de Cernon and the walled villages of Saint-Jean d'Alcas, La Couvertoirade and La Cavalerie, all supporting the order's work here since the middle of the last century. Guillaume de Saunhac tutors the commander of Sainte-Eulalie.
neighbours.secrets: Guillaume de Saunhac will be Master of the Temple in 1245.

neighbours.name: The Order of Aubrac
neighbours.summary: A small order of knights who guard pilgrims on the Way of St. James, south-west to Compostela and south-east to Rome. It was founded at the Dômerie d'Aubrac in the eleventh century and took the Rule of St. Augustine in 1162, and it keeps hospitals it calls commanderies at Bozouls, Millau, Nazac and Rodez. It competes with the Hospitallers, who would like to swallow it but have so far failed.

neighbours.name: The Troubadours of Rodez
neighbours.summary: Rodez is the local centre of the troubadour movement, under counts who sing themselves. The first troubadours were nobles, but now they come from all ranks of society. Fulk of Toulouse started as one before he repented, took orders and became bishop of Toulouse in 1205 and a force in the crusade. Renaud and Jean Marie of Stella Durus want to keep a troubadour at their covenant.

details.wants: Patrons, audiences and peace to sing in

neighbours.name: County of Millau
neighbours.summary:
A county that came to the crown of Aragon in the early twelfth century by the same marriage that brought it Gévaudan. It made pottery for the Roman Empire and still does; its craftsmen are famed for fine leather and for the Roquefort cheese they ripen in caves in the hills.

Huge ancient dolmens and menhirs are strewn across the land. The locals leave them alone, taking them for faerie homes and meeting places; they carry Faerie auras of 2 to 4, and the stronger the aura, the mightier the creature that lairs there.

neighbours.name: The Dolmens and Menhirs of Millau
neighbours.summary: Countless stone tables and standing stones across the Millau country, relics of its pagan past, shunned as the homes and gathering grounds of faeries. Each site has a Faerie aura of 2 to 4 (3 given here as typical), with stronger faeries at the stronger sites.

neighbours.name: The Roman Ruins across the Tarn
neighbours.summary: The remains of Roman Millau's potteries and town, mostly on the far bank of the Tarn from the living town and largely forgotten, though they hold a Magic aura of 3.

neighbours.name: Millau
neighbours.summary: A trading town where the Tarn and the Dourbie meet, crossed by a Roman bridge of seventeen spans over the Tarn, one of the largest in Mythic Europe, which puts it on an important trade route. Alphonso II of Aragon granted it a consular charter, so its consuls may tax and keep the law.
neighbours.ruler: Its consuls, under the crown of Aragon

neighbours.name: Notre-Dame-de-l'Espinasse, Millau
neighbours.summary: Millau's church, said to keep a piece of the Crown of Thorns: part of a rush with three pairs of thorns, broken from the great crown in Constantinople, in a small cage of gold mesh on a fine gold chain. The priest seldom takes it out for fear of harming it; it is carried before the people at Lent. It is an ordinary relic of Faith 3 with the saintly power to Cure Blindness. Divine aura 4.

relics.name: Fragment of the Crown of Thorns

neighbours.name: County of Gévaudan
neighbours.summary: A county of the crown of Aragon since 1112, once part of the diocese of Mende. Its north takes in some of the roughest country of the Massif Central: thinly peopled and notorious for fierce, clever wolves.

neighbours.name: The Barons of Gévaudan
neighbours.summary: Eight barons who hold Gévaudan for the crown of Aragon and have fought off the bishop of Mende's rule, though Louis VII's Golden Bull of Gévaudan gave the bishop temporal power there. The bishops tried again and again in the last century to take the county back.
neighbours.ruler: Eight barons, sworn to James of Aragon

neighbours.name: Bishop of Mende
neighbours.summary: The bishop whose diocese once took in Gévaudan and who holds Louis VII's Golden Bull granting him temporal power there; the barons sworn to Aragon refuse him.

neighbours.name: The Wolves' Cave Shrine
neighbours.summary: An ancient Gaulish cave shrine somewhere in the wilds of the Massif Central, with a Magic aura of 3, in country so empty a covenant could grow there far from the crusade, though specialists and rare supplies would be hard to get.
neighbours.secrets: The wolves that hunt travellers in these hills are not ordinary wolves: they are a little tribe of shape-changing werewolves, and this cave is their lair. Could they be tamed, and the shrine become a covenant?

neighbours.name: Lordship of Montpellier
neighbours.summary: The city of Montpellier and its lands, which passed to the crown of Aragon when Marie of Montpellier, its hereditary ruler, married Peter II in 1204; James was born there in 1208.

neighbours.name: Montpellier
neighbours.summary:
A spice-trading city the counts of Toulouse founded in 985, when pirate raids drove the coast-dwellers inland, and famous for tolerating Cathars, Jews and Muslims. It sits on two hills, Montpellier and Montpellieret, joined by steep streets, inside a wall with the Tour de la Babote and under a castle.

When Marie of Montpellier wed Peter II of Aragon in 1204 the match secured her right to rule and won the city a charter under which it picks twelve consuls each year. Notaries hold office for the city. The trobairitz Gormonda de Monpeslier, a fierce enemy of the Cathars, is its daughter.
neighbours.ruler: Twelve consuls chosen every year, under the crown of Aragon

neighbours.name: University of Montpellier
neighbours.summary: The school William VII of Montpellier founded, recognised as a university this very year, 1220, and famous for medicine (see Art & Academe). Ara Maxima Nova's magi have searched its books for the way to the Hesperides.

neighbours.name: The Wise of Provence
neighbours.summary: The yeshivas of Arles, Montpellier and Narbonne (Realms of Power: The Divine), where Jewish scholars interpret and set down Talmudic thought. Famous rabbis and kabbalists have studied at Narbonne: Moses ha-Darshan in the eleventh century, and in the twelfth Moses ben Joseph ben Merwan ha-Levi, thought by many the greatest Jewish mystic of his day. Called Hachmei Provence, they set the literary style and pedigree that remain the standard of Jewish scholarship.
neighbours.secrets: Story: a divinely blessed golem, servant of a kabbalist, breaks loose when a mob hangs its maker's grandson for something he never did, a lynching perhaps stirred up by a demon, a tainted jinn or a mischievous faerie. It beats its way through the town and will not stop until it finds the true culprit.

neighbours.name: County of Roussillon
neighbours.summary:
Named for Ruscino, a little stronghold where Gaulish chiefs met to weigh Hannibal's request for a parley. It is farming country known for vineyards and for woad, which is worked into a pale blue dye for cloth. The viscount owns some minor iron workings in the Pyrenean foothills and a gold mine of little yield near Saint-Jean-Pla-de-Corts.

As the border with Catalonia it bristles with fortifications: Castle Rodes stands on a high granite spur commanding the head of the Têt valley, and the southern port of Collioure, where the Templars built a castle above the bay in 1207, is a starting point for many crusaders. The Via Domitia comes down from the pass near Le Perthus through Perpignan.

neighbours.name: Sancho, count of Roussillon
neighbours.summary: Viscount Gerard II died heirless in 1172, and Roussillon passed to Alphonso II of Aragon by an agreement made beforehand with Gerard and his nobles, and Alphonso gave it to his brother Sancho. Sancho, count of Roussillon and Cerdagne, and his son Nuno Sanche, who holds Roussillon, Conflent, Vallespir and Cerdagne, are regents of Aragon for young James, who lives at Zaragoza.
neighbours.ruler: Sancho, with his son Nuno Sanche
neighbours.secrets: Sancho, backed by Nuno, now and then plots against the king he serves as regent.

neighbours.name: Perpignan
neighbours.summary:
Roussillon's capital on the Têt, its largest river, founded in the ninth century and a partly self-governing commune since 1197. It lives on wool, wine, cork, iron, leather and olive oil, behind high, thick walls. The viscount's compound holds a chapel, a hospital and the Château de Roussillon, whose round tower twenty paces high dominates it.

Ara Maxima Nova's vineyards and cork nurseries lie among the farming estates on its outskirts, and its magi slip into town for sweets and chess. In one of its taverns Ducaru of Stella Durus and Etienne of Ara Maxima Nova have been playing a game of chess for months, and Redcaps drop in to follow it and bet on the winner.

neighbours.name: Hospital of St. John the Baptist, Perpignan
neighbours.summary: The chapel and hospital in the viscount's compound, both under the patronage of the Baptist; the hospital cares for Perpignan's urban poor.

neighbours.name: The Poor Clares of Perpignan
neighbours.summary: The Order of Poor Sisters, living by Franciscan ideals, at work in the city and trying to found a convent there.

neighbours.name: The Abandoned Mine
neighbours.summary:
A small worked-out mine, which the book leaves for the storyguide to place (the iron workings in the Pyrenean foothills or the poor gold mine at Saint-Jean-Pla-de-Corts would serve). Covenfolk quarrying stone or picking over its tailings strike a new vein of gold or iron, perhaps with a visible pawn of vis.

Vis (unclaimed): every hundredth cartload of ore dug out by hand holds 2 pawns of Terram; ore taken out by magic holds none. Nobody knows how deep the vein goes, or whether the vis comes from the ore or from the labour of mining. The work could be dangerous for covenfolk new to it, the vis may end with the vein, and new digging may draw the local lord's eye.

neighbours.name: Raymond Roger I, count of Foix
neighbours.summary:
The counts of Foix served Toulouse in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Raymond Roger I, the fifth count, a troubadour and kinsman of Raimond VI, was held for a time in 1203 by the bishop of Urgell until Peter II of Aragon freed him, and he swore fealty to Peter. He is famous for generalship, chivalry, loyalty and fine clothes, and writes verse as well as paying for it. Not a Cathar himself, he married one and fought Simon de Montfort.

Foix belongs to the Pyrenean marches but its count is busy across the Toulousain and Narbonnais. Charlemagne founded the town; the Château de Foix, on a seventh-century stronghold, looms over it with a great round tower, held out against several crusader assaults, sheltered hunted Cathars, and is said to stand on rock riddled with caves.
neighbours.ruler: Raymond Roger I, fifth count of Foix

neighbours.name: Abbey of St. Volusien, Foix
neighbours.summary: A large red sandstone house of Augustinian canons founded in 1104, with a three-naved church keeping the bones of St. Volusien, patron of Foix, whom the Visigoths carried off and tortured to death. It is the spiritual and social centre of the town. Divine aura 4.

neighbours.name: The Gulf of Lion
neighbours.summary:
The Narbonnais shore, from Collioure past the mouths of the Aude and the Hérault toward the Rhône. Since the Umayyads took Iberia in the eighth century, Moorish corsairs have hunted these waters, and no crossing from the Catalan Sea to the Ligurian or Sardinian seas is safe from capture and slavery, so ships sail together in flotillas. Passing it takes a Moorish ship, magic, or a story (City & Guild).

A brutal corsair raids this coast, landing reavers to fall on caravans and pilgrims and taking captives for ransom. He has struck a bargain with a jinn called Howling Knife of the Dunes.
neighbours.secrets:
The Jinn Corsair (Faerie Might 20, Vim) looks like a handsome, grinning Maghrebi pirate with a brand on his left cheek, dressed in rich cloth, bearing a fine scimitar that looks like glass in the morning light. He is Muslim, proud and overconfident, and sells his service as a bodyguard; he has lost a charge only twice, once to a dragon and once to a Hermetic magus, perhaps of the players' own covenant. Powers: become a gritty desert whirlwind that can carry one person (Sirocco's Form, CrAu 50); find whoever an Arcane Connection he holds belongs to (InCo 20); sheathe his blade in white fire for +10 damage (CrIg 20); make one he touches invisible, though a shadow remains (PeIm 15). Scimitar: Attack +12, Damage +8, Defense +9, Init +3; Soak +6. He is bound by his name and serves whoever he has agreed to; failing a mission drives him to fury. His scimitar, weightless, holds one pawn apiece of Ignem, Auram, Imaginem and Corpus, and its bearer gains Puissant Single Weapon.

The jinn knows of the Order and has promised the pirates untold wealth if they bring him one particular magus; he has a second master, someone the players have angered.

neighbours.name: The Moorish Raiders
neighbours.summary: Corsairs based in the Maghreb, at Algiers, Marrakech, Tangier and the like, and in the nearby Balearics, who plunder Christian Iberia, Italy, Sicily and southern France, Narbonnais above all. The Balearic Crusade of 1115 stopped them for a year at most. The Italian cities, the Normans of Sicily, Aragon and Castile have tightened their hold on the western Mediterranean without ending the raids. Ara Maxima Nova buys some slaves from Arab merchants.

details.wants: Plunder, captives to ransom or sell

neighbours.name: The Notaries of Narbonnais
neighbours.summary: A profession grown from the remnants of Roman law. Notaries arose in Narbonnais in the 1140s, writing up charters and contracts alongside the consular governments of the communes. At first they named themselves; now secular and Church lords appoint them, making notary a public office whose authenticated documents stand in court. They are paid at Christmas by their employers, may not be clergy, answer to secular law, and hold office only for a given realm or town, such as the county of Nîmes or Montpellier. Their patron is St. Genesius of Lodève.

details.rules: Lay office only: a notary who takes the tonsure leaves the notariate
details.offers: Drawn contracts, witnessed charters, verified documents, a seal

neighbours.name: The Via Domitia
neighbours.summary:
The ancient road the Romans paved: from the Pyrenean pass near Le Perthus through Perpignan, over a bridge of seven arches into Narbonne, on through Béziers, Montpellier and Nîmes into the Kingdom of Arelat, north at Céreste into the Piedmont, and over the Alps by the Col de Montgenèvre, the lowest main pass between France and Italy. Locals believe Heracles walked it on his labours, and Hannibal certainly marched it toward Rome. In Roman times mansiones, staging posts a day's journey apart, gave travellers rest and food.

Ara Maxima Nova guards the road jealously and uses it in its initiations and rites; its magi often challenge to certamen any magus they think is studying the road's secrets rather than simply travelling it. Stella Durus respects its claim.
neighbours.secrets:
Heraclean vis: someone who walks the whole road from the Le Perthus pass to the Col de Montgenèvre carrying a lion's skin, and camps for the night at six of the old mansio sites, finds 6 pawns of Intellego vis in the skin. One site is an open lot inside Narbonne, and Ara Maxima Nova watches the road closely. Its magi do not yet know of this vis, but some local faeries do and might trade the knowledge.

An Iberian Redcap carrying Tibaut's sealed letter to Beatrice died of an ambush by crusader camp followers in the wilds along the road; the letter is still in his satchel (see The Serpent's Venom).

neighbours.name: The River Aude
neighbours.summary: The river that runs down from the Pyrenees past Carcassonne to Narbonne and the sea, giving the city its port. A powerful magic spirit, a daimon, dwells in it. Stella Durus sits on its left bank, and Marcella of Bonisagus has studied its spirit for years.
neighbours.secrets: Marcella hopes to tap the Aude's spirit for vis without killing it. One of the paths open to her is a ritual murder of the spirit for a single great store of vis; if that is done, the river will silt up over the years and Narbonne will decline as a port.

neighbours.name: The Villa of Stella Durus
neighbours.summary: An old Roman villa on the left bank of the Aude, just outside Narbonne, altered, enlarged and rebuilt many times, with an old manor farm. Nothing about it stands out and it is hardly defended. Neighbours take it for the house of a merchant who travels a great deal, or of a petty lord away on crusade, and leave it alone. A Roman mithraeum once stood in its basements, which hold a Magic aura of 2.

neighbours.name: The Villa of Ara Maxima Nova
neighbours.summary: A cluster of small buildings round a modest villa, with vineyards and cork nurseries, among the many farming estates on the outskirts of Perpignan. It does not hide from its neighbours but keeps a carefully ordinary face. The book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: Arelat
neighbours.summary:
The Tribunal's eastern march: the lands of the old Kingdom of Lower Burgundy, bounded on the west by the Rhone (save the little County of Viviers, Beaucaire and the Lyonnais, which lie across it) and running east along the Mediterranean shore to the Maritime Alps a little past Nice. Its north-eastern edge is vague, somewhere beyond the Grande Chartreuse where the Viennois meets Savoy and the Greater Alps; by custom the Tropaeum Alpium marks its eastern limit. Rome settled here before anywhere else outside Italy, and the churches and towns of the Middle Ages stand on a carpet of Roman and Gallic ruins. Franks, Lombards and Saracens came in turn until Charles Martel conquered it; in 1220 it is calmer, and a heartland of the troubadours.

The country is hot and poor, scoured by the Mistral, and known for wine, honey, limes and olives. Frederick II, the Emperor, is nominally King of Arles but acts only through his viceroy at Arles; the strongest magnate is the Catalan Ramon Berenguer V, Count of Provence and now of Forcalquier, back from captivity in Aragon since 1219; and the young Count of Toulouse still claims the March of Provence, which its lords honour when it suits them. Much of the land answers to petty lords or to chartered towns, above all Arles and Avignon, the great communes of the river. The Albigensian Crusade has not ravaged it, though some communes, and perhaps some magi, have quietly helped both sides.

This was once part of the Lotharingian Tribunal; when the Grand Tribunal of 898 sent its northern covenants to Normandy and the Rhine, the remnant along the Rhone and in the Toulousain became the Provençal Tribunal. Proud heirs of the Roman Provincia, its first covenants kept their Latin names for every official document, a custom still followed. Its early magi left many ruins, monuments to how hard Hermetic cooperation can be, until the heirs of the fallen covenants pooled their holdings in the Coenobium, which now has a grip on nearly every easily reached magical resource in the region and dominates its hedge wizards. Its magi care little for the Rhine's Lotharingian Movement.

Unclaimed or contested vis in Arelat (each described in its place): the yew of the Isle d'Yf (Intellego, with the ruin of Yf), the monthly almond blossom of Ste Marguerite at Lérins (Mentem, Divine-tainted), the blood-red ford of St Gilles (Corpus, Infernal-tainted), the golden goat's wool in the Alpilles (Imaginem), the field of the Golden Court of 1174 (Faerie vis, suspected), the Source du Groseau below Ventoux (Aquam), and the ruined mills of Barbegal north of Arles, with a Magic aura of 5 and three magical wheels still lost.
neighbours.secrets: Fraxinetum Redux, heirs of the raider covenant the Coenobium destroyed, keep a hidden base on the Hyères islands, and a Tytalus eremite, Aucassin, lives in a regio under Beaucaire. Individual Tytali may have reason to work their way into the Coenobium and undermine it, which could set off a conflict across the Order.

neighbours.name: The Rhone
neighbours.summary:
'The Bruiser' to its boatmen: a river of fierce currents, shoals and spring floods, navigable by barge up to about Macon. Joined by the Saone at Lyon, it runs down the great trench between the Massif Central and the Alpine foothills and is the south-western frontier of the Empire. Only four bridges cross it: Lyon's ancient bridge on oak piles, Vienne's Roman one of stone, Avignon's newer Pont St Bénezet, and a lesser wooden bridge at Arles to Trinquetaille. Going down from Macon to Arles takes about three weeks, and the trip back a week or two longer, the barges hauled by horse teams or helped by magic; at Arles cargoes go onto small sailing barges for the sea.

Barge trains of five to seven craft, towed by fifty or more horses along the banks, carry the bulk goods; nobles ride the water coaches, under sail or drawn by horses, which Jerbiton magi prefer to magic. Boats bear crosses and holy signs against harm, and many magi hide small wards in the designs.

Lesser drac haunt the darker reaches of its tributaries: young Faerie drakes (Faerie Might 15, rising by 10 at their place of power), greenish-black, long-bodied, with webbed legs like a flamingo's and lacy blue fins for wings. They lure washerwomen, children and vagrants to watery lairs with illusions, can take human size, and let anyone they grapple breathe underwater; they feed on the fear their stories spread, and some live among people disguised as boatmen, laundresses or merchants. Each carries 3 pawns of Imaginem vis in its eyes. A human can hold a drac's jaws shut, since the muscles that open them are weak.

Gervase of Tilbury's Otia imperialia, an encyclopedia of myth and marvels written at Arles between 1210 and 1214, tells of the drac's recent return and names two ways into its lair, a pool outside the north gate of Arles and a well at Beaucaire; it serves as four tractatus of Quality 6 (Provençal Lore, Faerie Lore, Infernal Lore and Magic Lore). The Redcaps think a further entrance lies in some Magic aura on a lonelier stretch of the river, and that all of them open on a great web of regiones under the valley, which might serve as a magical road; those who walk it hear inhuman breathing and feel hunted.
neighbours.secrets: The Coenobium keeps at least one barge as a floating laboratory, moored along the banks or tributaries wherever a good Magic aura lies.

neighbours.name: Pont Saint-Bénezet
neighbours.summary:
Avignon's bridge: twenty-two stone arches across the low Isle de Barthelasse in midstream, unpaved but sound, with a drawbridge at the eastern end to keep the Porte du Rhone shut and a great gatehouse still unfinished. Over the third pier from the east bank is a small chapel of St Nicholas of Myra holding St Bénezet's body and relics, beloved of the Rhone boatmen; its Divine aura of 4 covers only the first few piers. Its doorkeeper, Jorin, a former boatman and retired Redcap, reports to the Coenobium.

Under the first arch, the only one on the eastern shore, is a piece of Roman temple said to have been set there by the saint: a small Magic lacuna of 4, smothered by the chapel's aura by day but felt at night. Past the chapel the bridge is beyond the Divine aura of 3 thrown by the city and the abbey across the river, and the bound spirits of the Rhone flowing under its arches raise a weak Magic aura of 2 there.

neighbours.name: The Drac's Well at Beaucaire
neighbours.summary:
A disused well in Beaucaire's old marketplace, with a weak Magic aura (the book gives no strength). Local legend tells of the Drac, a cruel sorcerer-dragon of the river older than the Order, who drew mothers and little children to his lair beneath the water, walked unseen among the townsfolk, and is blamed for some three thousand dead knights and villagers. No tale says he was slain, so he was thought to have died of age, until a run of disappearances about ten years ago; none have been reported for some years, and folk are forgetting, but the well is still said to reach his lair.

Nicolette, a young woman of the town, tells anyone who will listen her dreams of dragons and drowned kingdoms. Old folk say she once vanished for seven years and came back remembering nothing, not even the baby son she left; her husband and grown boy turn the talk when strangers press.
neighbours.secrets:
Beneath the well opens the underwater regio web that runs under the Rhone and the Drac river, with a powerful Magic aura. Aucassin of Tytalus has his sanctum there and revived the Drac legend to cover his kidnappings. Cave paintings within, with the regio itself, make up a Mystery Initiation Script to mature a human heir of the Drac into a true elder drac; a deeper level, aligned to Imaginem, opens on the Magic Realm, where a sleeping dragon Vestige like a giant drac guards the far side. Aucassin has taken some odd vis from beyond it but dares not face the Vestige yet.

Living under compulsion in the caves are Aucassin's abducted servants, among them a lavender-seller as wet nurse and a young scribe once used by Alazais, made to teach his sickly Gifted captive, 'Le Petit', Latin and the liberal arts. Nicolette may be a former drac bride freed to spread tales, or one of Aucassin's escaped grogs.

neighbours.name: The Field of the Golden Court
neighbours.summary:
Meadows just north of Beaucaire where Henry II, then Count of Provence, held a court in 1174 to mark Narbonne's reconciliation with the King of Aragon, and where (by Abbot Geoffrey of Vigeois's flattering chronicle) a hundred thousand knights gathered. Most were faeries reveling in the foudat, the deliberate folly that troubadour culture breeds: thirty thousand gold sous of glamour were ploughed into the ground, and herds of faerie cattle roasted over costly wax and pitch-pine torches. The faeries crowned Guilhem Mita 'King of the Minstrels' with a gold crown sent by Sorgest, the faerie-blooded Countess of Urgell.

Each anniversary, faeries in the likeness of the troubadours and nobles of that day replay the feast and try to pull mortals into new versions of it. The Faerie aura of 3 rises to 5 on the anniversary. Minor demons of envy, greed and lust, shed from the crusading army's wake, have lately settled round about. The Coenobium suspects the field could yield plentiful, renewable Faerie-tainted vis, and may send would-be members to look into it.

neighbours.name: The Tarasque's Lair
neighbours.summary:
A cave in the hills outside Tarascon where the Tarasque laired: a six-legged amphibious beast that St Martha tamed and the villagers of Nerluc then slew in cowardly fashion in AD 48. Its remains are long scattered, but the cave runs down into flooded passages that may join others in the region. The residual Magic aura is 2, with stronger regiones believed to lie deeper.

Lesser kin of the beast may lurk there. A small tarasque (Magic Might 20) is a winged, scaly ox with a lizard-like lion's head, six taloned legs, a tortoise's shell and a leathery tail, about fifteen paces long, smoke curling from its jaws: it flies though its wings should not carry it, breathes a long gout of fire, cannot be harmed by fire or want, and is cowed by sincere holy display, as hymns once mesmerised its ancestor. Its shell holds 4 pawns of Animal vis.

Just north of the town, by a small island, Hannibal fought the Volcae at the Rhone crossing; on clear moonlit nights boatmen see giant elephant skeletons on the riverbed and huge ghostly beasts marching under the current.

neighbours.name: The Alyscamps
neighbours.summary:
The old Roman necropolis of Arles along the road east, famous for its crypts and tombs; coffins once floated down the Rhone from all over Europe, steered by boatmen who did not always deliver the valuables with them. Its glory faded when the relics of St Trophimus went to the cathedral in 1152, and townsfolk now take its stones for building while the council gives sarcophagi away to honoured visitors.

The spirit masters of Elisii Campi lived in its crypts in the tenth century, hid through the Schism War, and were driven out when the Coenobium stirred up the townsfolk with rumours of diabolists under the necropolis. Many sarcophagi still hold their enchantments and traps; one that falls into a covenant's hands could lead to a hidden covenant in the Verdon Gorge, or to blood on the Coenobium's past.

neighbours.name: Pont Flavian
neighbours.summary:
A single-arched Roman bridge between two triumphal arches, carrying the Via Julia Augusta over the Touloubre near St Chamas. It has stood over a thousand years partly thanks to the faerie ogre living under it (Faerie Might 20, 30 at his best), who takes a toll of sheep and beer, or wine and a sheep a wagon, or a sack of coin, and eats those who sneak across or damage the bridge. He is a huge boar-headed brute with clawed hands and amber tusks, clubbing with a root-spiked tree stump, throwing stones he pulls from the earth, moving soundlessly, and able to seem a standing stone; heads hang at his belt, among them a skull in a net that holds 4 pawns of Corpus vis and makes its bearer Tough. He claims to be cousin to the Boar King of Normandy.

He lately caught a lost Redcap, who promised a ransom from the magi; the ogre hid him in an oubliette only he can open and sent a shepherd boy for the wizards, eating a sheep for each day past the fourth. If the ogre dies first, the Redcap rots unfound.

neighbours.name: The Alpilles
neighbours.summary:
A range of limestone teeth at the northern edge of the Crau, so like the Alps in little that locals call them the Alps' children. Wild and untouched, they rise above St-Rémy and hold both Magic and Faerie auras with their creatures.

Here roams le Chèvre d'Or, the Golden Goat, said to guard the treasure cave of the first Caliph of Cordoba, Abd al-Rahman III, whose daughter she is: a goat with a fiery golden coat and a gold coronet on ebony horns, who seems trapped and begs, in Arabic and then Occitan, to be freed, and if ignored becomes a beautiful Saracen princess promising her treasure. She is a powerful nymph (or, if the storyguide prefers, a Spirit of Deceit) who keeps the way into a treasure regio, perhaps at the foot of the Garagai, in the Val d'Enfer, or in any gully of the Provençal foothills; it lets people in but not out, and without Second Sight a lover may wander its layers for ever. The few youths who escape lose their wits or souls, or come back as impostors.

Shepherds find strands of her golden wool on the bushes: accrued Imaginem vis, unclaimed, which an aesthete of the Coenobium might set a would-be member to gather.

neighbours.name: The Val d'Enfer
neighbours.summary:
A rocky valley under the plateau of Les Baux, lined with sinister caves, under an Infernal aura of 2. The caves lead into a Tartaran regio where lesser demons of pride and ambition dwell, the ones that drove the lords of Baux into their wars over the centuries. The Golden Goat's treasure regio may open here.

Carved into the rock below the valley is the Tremais, a rough sculpture of three figures most take for Lazarus, Mary Magdalene and Martha: a minor pilgrimage shrine with a Divine aura of 4, set inside a wider Faerie aura of 2, for the carving first honoured the Roman general Marius, his wife and his Syrian sibyl Martha before missionaries claimed it.

neighbours.name: The Camargue
neighbours.summary:
The marshy triangle between the Rhone's two last branches, entered from Trinquetaille, Arles's unwalled suburb on the right bank, where the Coenobium's Factory stands. The Bjornaer of the Birds of Camargue lived here until they joined the Coenobium in 970.

Two Bjornaer, nominally the Coenobium's guests, live on the edge of Trinquetaille and spend most of their time in the marsh: little Bubulcus, usually an egret, riding his bull, and Elornis One-Leg, a greater flamingo. Both know of the legendary horses of the Camargue and the Great Stallion who leads them, but have little to do with them.

neighbours.name: The Ford of St Gilles
neighbours.summary: A ford on the Rhone just outside St Gilles where the papal legate Peter of Castelnau was killed in 1208, by a demon or by one of Raimond VI's men. It is stained by an Infernal aura of 3. On the anniversary the river runs red as blood, and small skull-shaped pebbles yield several pawns of Corpus vis, always Infernally tainted. Unclaimed.

neighbours.name: The Arch of Orange
neighbours.summary: Tiberius's triumphal arch, now built into Orange's walls as its north gate astride the old Via Agrippa. A Magic aura of 2 flickers up at night when the Divine aura fades. Some magi think it may keep secrets of the Mercurians' old road magic, and Neo-Mercurians and members of the Cult of Mercury quietly study its inscriptions and stones. Nearby, the ruins of one of the finest Roman theatres outside Italy, shut by the Christians in 391, lie as the barbarians left them.

neighbours.name: The Plaine de la Crau
neighbours.summary:
A stony plain on the Via Domitia, of great interest to Ara Maxima Nova: legend says Heracles, driving Geryon's cattle home, was set on here by the giants Bergion and Ligur, sons of Poseidon, and when he prayed to Zeus the plain rained the rocks he hurled to beat them. Its round stones make good sling and catapult shot.

Among them, now and then, is a perfectly round sling stone that is Terram vis. The Coenobium's grogs gather a handful each year with minor enchanted devices under apprentices' eyes, a tedious chore kept for troublemakers and idlers.

neighbours.name: The Frioul Islands
neighbours.summary: Four small, uninhabited islands off Marseille. Smugglers, pirates and Saracen raiders from their nest in the Hyères moor at Pomègues and Ratonneau, the two largest; Tiboulen is the tiniest. The fourth, the Isle d'Yf, with its old yew grove and the ruins of the Diedne covenant of Yf, is described with that ruin.
neighbours.secrets: The magi of Fraxinetum Redux harvest vis on the small islands of the coast, Yf among them.

neighbours.name: The Massif des Maures
neighbours.summary: A granite upland between Hyères and Fréjus, strange among Provence's limestone hills and dark with forests, named for the Saracen privateers who held the coast and the Alpine passes from the eighth to the tenth century. Above St Tropez, almost unreachable among its crystalline peaks, lies La Garde-Freinet, the razed site of Fraxinetum amid cork, oak and chestnut woods, still with a Magic aura of 4 and the ruins of the covenant fort. A palisade of close-set ash trees planted by its Herbam masters rings the grounds, and the remnants of their defensive rituals make the bigger ashes beat back intruders, so peasants call the place haunted and leave it unlooted.

neighbours.name: The Hyères Islands
neighbours.summary:
The Stoechades of Pliny and the Greeks, opposite old Olbia, known for slopes covered in lavender. A monastery holds the big eastern island, the Ile du Levant, while pirates haunt the quiet coves of Port-Cros and Porquerolles; the Giens peninsula to the west is cut off except at the lowest tides, a fourth island most of the year. Charlemagne brought the lavender (stoechas) to the mainland, and it is now in every monastic physic garden and in the folk magic of the south-east (+3 to cleansing, purifying or healing, +5 against evil spirits).

Lavender of Virtue holds a pawn of Rego vis a bunch. Dried in an open barn through the winter Mistral, tied in a posy and steeped a season in asp venom, it becomes an amulet that gives a wearer without Magic Resistance Greater Immunity to one major disease while its scent can be smelled; it lasts a year and warps its wearer as a constant low-power effect, and hung over a lintel it protects the sick recovering in the room beyond. Unclaimed.
neighbours.secrets: The heirs of Fraxinetum keep their base here, among the lavender of the pirate isles, and sponsor raids on the coast and on Catalan and Genoese shipping.

neighbours.name: Mount Ventoux
neighbours.summary:
'The Home of the Winds', the bald mountain at Provence's northern edge, long feared as the source of the Mistral. Chapels stand on its lower slopes, among them two chapels and a watchtower at Beaumont-du-Ventoux and the great monastery of Notre-Dame-du-Groseau. The upper slopes have a Magic aura of 7, rising to a regio of 9 near the summit, where the endless gale lets nothing grow. There dwell air spirits of many strengths under a great daimon called Ventoux, who now and then lets his lesser kin loose on the country below.

Calais filius Septentrio of Bonisagus, a Rhine magus staying with the Coenobium who calls himself Master of the Winds, made a sanctum in a cave just below the summit to win the daimon over as its Spirit Votary. That angered the Mistrau ('the Master'), an ancient Faerie lord who embodies every Provençal tale of the mistral: he has sealed the spirits' regio, which has made this season unusually mild, and Calais is trapped inside fighting Ventoux's angry servants. His hosts expected him back last season. To get in, one must beat one of the Mistrau's champions at catching two fleeting things out of Arcadia: winter's dying breath and spring's first sigh.

levels.name: The Home of the Winds
levels.notes: Above the gravelly summit, where the wind never stops: the realm of many air spirits ruled by the great daimon Ventoux, now sealed by the Mistrau with Calais of Bonisagus inside.

neighbours.secrets: The storyguide may make the daimon or the Mistrau an Infernal spirit of the Order of Aerial Powers posing as Faerie, hoping by a pact to spread corruption through every elementalist tradition in the Order; the prayers of the monks of Notre-Dame-du-Groseau have partly held it in.

neighbours.name: The Source du Groseau
neighbours.summary: A magical spring gushing from a cliff north of Ventoux, sacred to the Celtic spring god Groselos, and a possible source of Aquam vis. Unclaimed.

neighbours.name: The Garagai Gorge
neighbours.summary:
A chasm near Montagne Sainte-Victoire, outside Aix. After Marius crushed the Teutones there in 102 BC, so many that the Campi Putridi were fattened for years, legend says three hundred captive chieftains were driven into the gorge at the urging of his Syrian sibyl Martha, and each anniversary their spirits rise from the floor to relive the defeat. The lip has an Infernal aura of 2, stronger lower down, where unexplored Tartaran regiones lead, some say, to a mouth of Hell at the very bottom. Some tales put the Golden Goat's treasure cave here.

The ghosts are not Infernal but Magic, Teutonic kin of House Tremere's ghostly soldiers; questioned, they might reveal the lost tradition of Martha, who may have been of a lineage like the Canaanite necromancers. Even before the slaughter, prophetic spirits were said to rise from the depths, best treated as Spirits of Deceit, and local masques or necromantic magi may still call them.

neighbours.name: The Sanctuary of Venus on Ste Marguerite
neighbours.summary:
The Iles de Lérins have been a land of monks since St Honoratus drove off their venomous snakes in the fifth century; the snakes never returned, but the Saracens did, killing Abbot St Porcarius in the eighth. On the smaller island, under the sister convent of Ste Marguerite, a cave network hides a little sanctuary of Venus that the fourteenth abbot, St Nazarius, failed to destroy; it keeps a weak Magic aura of 2.

Also on the island is an almond tree that flowers every month: its crushed blossoms give 1 pawn of Mentem vis a month, Divinely tainted. Unclaimed.

neighbours.name: The Tropaeum Alpium
neighbours.summary:
The Trophy of Augustus at La Turbie: a round arcaded monument to Rome's defeat of the Gaulish tribes, once the edge of Roman Italy on the Via Julia Augusta, later a fortress and refuge. By tradition it marks the Tribunal's easternmost limit, though the town is under Genoa and counted part of Liguria in speech and politics. Christian mobs, taking it for a pagan temple, smashed most of the statue of Augustus inside, and villagers have carried off its stones; whatever magic they hold is drowned by the Divine aura of 3 of the nearby church of St Michael.

The mostly Mercurian magi of short-lived Turris Mascis, the Tower of the Masques, studied the monument, but what they learned is lost.

neighbours.name: Lower Burgundy
neighbours.summary: The north of Arelat: part of the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy (Cisjurania) that Boso of Provence proclaimed at Arles in 879, then of the reunited Kingdom of Arelat from 933, and under the Emperor Conrad II from 1032, though it slips ever further from imperial control. Like the Duchy of Burgundy in the Normandy Tribunal, it is known more for cathedrals, monasteries and pilgrimages than for trade. It is quite apart from the old Kingdom of Upper Burgundy north of the Jura and the Free County of Burgundy, which lie in the Tribunal of the Greater Alps. Beatrice of Albon, Dauphine of Viennois, rules here, while the prince-archbishop of Vienne disputes the land with her line.

neighbours.name: Notre Dame de Vie at Vienne
neighbours.summary: A church at Vienne that hides the colonnaded Temple of Augustus and Livia, with a Magic aura of 3, thought once to have been an important Mercurian site. Nearby a truncated pyramid called Pilate's Tomb is said to mark where Pilate's body was sunk in the river, until it stirred up evil spirits in the water and was taken out. A Roman theatre lies on Mont Pipet to the east, and old roads and aqueducts run on the city's edge.

neighbours.name: The Grande Chartreuse
neighbours.summary:
The Carthusians' motherhouse in the mountains above Grenoble: a cloister of separate cells, each a two-storey hermitage with its own walled garden off a long corridor. The monks' simple devotion gives the motherhouse a Divine aura of 7; the valley has 3. Several choir monks are unGifted Ascetics of a Holy Tradition; the prior and at least one other have True Faith, two elder brothers are skilled mythic herbalists, and the old hunchbacked cellarer, Salvatore, has the Blatant Gift.

Its newest retreatant is Romualdus, once a Jerbiton magus, now the novice Brother Thomas, who has cut himself off from his old sodales.
neighbours.secrets: Romualdus has found that Brother Jude, a shy, clumsy young novice, holds True Faith as well as the Gift. He has befriended him and fears the boy will be claimed as a Hermetic apprentice if word gets out; he might seek a Bonisagus to intervene and then help train Jude himself, at the cost of his new vows.

neighbours.name: The Lac du Bourget
neighbours.summary: A beautiful lake just north of Aix-les-Bains, the Roman spa whose hot springs in the foothills of the Jura and the Alps still draw travellers. Fed by the Leysse, it is said to be the largest and deepest lake of the area, with an Aquam regio deep in its waters. Some magi report the elemental Men of the Lake here, unconfirmed.

neighbours.name: The Coenobium's Avignon chapter (Sub Pontem)
neighbours.summary:
The heart of the covenant, the old Sub Pontem: council rooms and guest quarters dug under the lightly wooded Isle de Barthelasse, the shifting midstream island above the Pont St Bénezet. The island is in effect a great lacuna in the city's Dominion, with a Magic aura of 2, which is 3 at the island's northern end, where most of the visiting magi's laboratories lie underground; the Rhone's floods sometimes make that hard. Only this northern site has an Aegis of the Hearth, renewed at the summer solstice rather than in winter.

Nicodemus's underground laboratory opens under the bridge's second pier; the magi of old Sub Pontem still work their urban magic on the arches beyond the chapel, and one of the covenant's laboratory barges usually lies moored below a western pier. The consuls' townhouses in and around Avignon sit in the city's small lacunae and rely on weaker wards. Patrons have transport magic tied by Arcane Connection to the main council chamber, to come to a meeting at short notice.

neighbours.name: The Coenobium's Arles chapter (St Cyprian's)
neighbours.summary: The Mercer House of the Tribunal, in Les Arènes: the Roman arena of Arles, stripped for building stone and now a maze of hovels, churches and illicit trades that respectable folk avoid after dark. It passes for a pilgrims' inn of St Cyprian and is in truth a brothel, nominally owned by Alazais; the covenant's Redcaps and Jerbiton magi meet here and often stay for its earthier pleasures. Below the inn and the client rooms, chambers serve more discreet business. The city's Divine aura keeps any Magic aura from forming, so there is no Aegis; an archway carved with magical inscriptions links one chamber to the rooms under the Isle de Barthelasse.

neighbours.name: The Coenobium's Trinquetaille chapter (the Factory)
neighbours.summary: A great warehouse at Trinquetaille, at the gate of the Camargue, holding the covenant's mundane wealth behind what look like ordinary merchants' stores. It runs several levels underground, with a heavily warded area inside a second Aegis for dangerous and exotic goods and captive creatures. Only patrons join its Aegis ritual, and the First Consul keeps a close hand on its few tokens each year. The heavier processes behind the covenant's wealth are worked here, magic helping or replacing the usual methods, hidden by subtle wards and by traps that wipe memories.

neighbours.name: The Coenobium's Toulon chapter
neighbours.summary:
A small chapter house below Mount Faron at Toulon, on the site of the old Flambeau covenant of Telo Martius. Toulon has made dyes since the Phoenicians: its beaches are among the few sources of the murex shellfish for imperial purple, and the hillside oaks keep the kermes beetle for a crimson nearly as precious. Aloysius Porphyri, a retired Redcap and unGifted alchemist, runs the chapter, oversees both harvests and one of the dye works of the covenant's factory outside the town.

Purple once went only to the Byzantine emperors; now only part goes east, the covenant keeping some for magic (purple: +10 royalty, +7 rule and authority, +5 controlling people). The crimson is sold widely and loved by hoplites and Flambeau (+7 violence, +4 courage and martyrdom, +3 sin). Magic makes the extraction cheaper than any rival's, but the covenant takes care not to flood the market. A rare shell or beetle holds a little Imaginem vis.

neighbours.name: King of Arles
neighbours.summary: Frederick II, the Emperor, holds the rather hollow title of King of Arles, ruling the kingdom of Arelat and Provence in name. In practice he has little sway there, exercised through his viceroy at Arles, the young Prince of Orange. Lower Burgundy grows ever more independent of him, and the Rhone's boatmen and the Coenobium's servants count themselves part of no distant Empire.

neighbours.name: Count of Provence
neighbours.summary: Ramon Berenguer V, a Catalan of the house of Barcelona, Count of Provence and now of Forcalquier too, the region's strongest magnate; he was freed in 1219 from imprisonment in Aragon. His mother Garsenda's marriage to Alfonso in 1209 brought him the wide Forcalquier inheritance. Aix, the old Roman Aquae Sextiae by its thermal spring, is his recently chosen capital, and his house's backing made Marseille a great port again. Avignon owes him no allegiance.

neighbours.name: Countess of Forcalquier
neighbours.summary: Countess Garsenda governs the county along the Durance from the citadel on its steep conical hill, as regent; her marriage to Alfonso in 1209 added her inheritance to her son's lands as Count of Provence. A trobairitz in her own right and a famous patron of troubadours across the south, she is said to have powers beyond the ordinary troubadour's gift of inspiring song.
neighbours.secrets: Among her rumoured lovers is at least one Jerbiton magus of the Coenobium.

neighbours.name: Prince of Orange
neighbours.summary: Raymond I of Baux, young prince of Orange, a Celtic oppidum and then a colony of Caesar's veterans that the Baux have held since the Kingdom of Arles broke up in 1033; Frederick I raised the county to a little principality in 1163. Raymond acts as the Emperor's viceroy at Arles and still claims that office, which his father William, a troubadour, held until he died in an Avignon prison in 1218; but the town's commune limits his power sharply.

neighbours.name: Lord of Baux
neighbours.summary:
Hugh III, son of Bertrand, Seigneur of Baux, whose fortress was razed in 1162 at the end of the Baussenque Wars against the Catalan counts. He lives mostly in bustling Marseille, which he holds as viscount for the Emperor. His kin include the Prince of Orange and much of Provence's lesser nobility, and his younger cousin Marcus is the wizard Balthazar of the Coenobium, through whom Hugh keeps close ties to the covenant; his young son Barral deeply distrusts his father's dealings with wizards.

The Baux claim descent from Balthazar, one of the three wise kings, and bear the Star of Bethlehem; their deeds have been less than Christian. The shield shown follows the later blazon, gules a star argent (of sixteen rays, which the app draws as a plain star).
neighbours.secrets: The Gift turns up unusually often in the family; the Coenobium encourages the Balthazar legend among the nobles to its own ends.

neighbours.name: Dauphine of Viennois
neighbours.summary: Beatrice of Albon, Dauphine of Viennois and Countess of Albon, whose grandson Hugh IV, aged eight, is Duke of Burgundy in the Normandy Tribunal. The dauphins keep challenging the prince-archbishop of Vienne for control of the region; it has not yet come to blows, but threatens to.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Vienne
neighbours.summary: Vienne, once capital of the Allobroges and a great Roman colony, is the seat of the archbishop of northern Arelat. Jean de Bernin, its prince-archbishop, is lawful count of the area for the Emperor but is constantly challenged by the dauphins.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St Trophime, Arles
neighbours.summary: The cathedral of Arles, which has held the relics of St Trophimus since they were taken from the Alyscamps in 1152, draining the old necropolis of its importance. The city's Divine aura is why the Coenobium's Mercer House can raise no Aegis.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St André
neighbours.summary: A prosperous abbey-town on Mont Andaon at the western end of Avignon's bridge, commanding the road to the commune and lodging pilgrims bound for Santiago. It keeps the relics of St Casarie, a Visigothic princess who lived as a hermit in the sixth century, under a strong Divine aura of 4. The abbot, a distant kinsman of the Baux and one of the greatest landowners nearby, is more open than most churchmen and sometimes receives the more respectable hedge wizards. Magi who refuse the Coenobium's hospitality may ask him for lodging in the aptly named Tower of Sorcerers, discreetly, or risk the bishop's anger and the Coenobium's interest.
neighbours.secrets: He secretly keeps on good terms with the Coenobium, and Marcus d'Les Baux has meddled on his behalf.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St Ruf
neighbours.summary: The canons of St Rufus, Avignon's patron saint, keep an abbey, church and hospice just outside the town near the Rhone; its grounds have a Divine aura of 3.

neighbours.name: Abbey of St Gilles
neighbours.summary: A Benedictine house grown from the seventh-century hermitage of St Giles, the first halt on the Via Tolosana from Arles and a day's walk on the Way of St James; abbey and town are a pilgrimage in their own right, and the birthplace and family lands of the recent counts of Toulouse. Barren women come to the saint's crypt to pray for children, and cripples on his feast, the first of September.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Psalmody
neighbours.summary: The abbey near the Petit Rhone that owns the land of the ruins of Castra Peccaius, which the Coenobium leases through its dependants for the salt pond inside. If history runs its course the monks will sell it to King Louis to found Aigues-Mortes for his crusade, and corrupt captains may then grab the salt pans, and the vis.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Lérins
neighbours.summary: The fortified monastery on the Ile St-Honorat, which the book calls Cistercian, ruling the walled town on the mainland under the watchtower on the Suquet. Pilgrims flock to St Honoratus: some count the journey equal to one to the Holy Land, and it has trained remarkable clerics, perhaps St Patrick. Its sister convent of Ste Marguerite stands on the smaller island.

neighbours.name: Notre-Dame-du-Groseau
neighbours.summary: The large monastery on Ventoux's lower slopes, whose prayers and hymns, if the mountain's powers are Infernal, have partly held them in.

neighbours.name: Order of the Carthusians
neighbours.summary: Founded in 1084 by the hermit St Bruno of Cologne under its own statutes, motto 'the Cross stands firm while the world turns'.
